title: 'The best club in the world to be at' - Gvardiol signs new deal
description: Manchester City defender Josko Gvardiol has officially signed a new five-year contract to extend his stay at Etihad Stadium.  The 24-year-old, who joined the club from RB Leipzig in August 2023, has since made 122 appearances and won six trophies under previous manager Pep Guardiola.  Gvardiol contributed two goals and five assists across 25 appearances last season, while also representing Croatia at his second World Cup this summer.
fullText:
Manchester City defender Josko Gvardiol has officially signed a new five-year contract to extend his stay at Etihad Stadium.

The 24-year-old, who joined the club from RB Leipzig in August 2023, has since made 122 appearances and won six trophies under previous manager Pep Guardiola.

Gvardiol contributed two goals and five assists across 25 appearances last season, while also representing Croatia at his second World Cup this summer.

He also played a pivotal role as Manchester City became the first team in English football to secure four consecutive top-flight titles in 2023-24.

"As soon as I knew City wanted to renew my contract, I felt straight away that it was what I wanted," Gvardiol said. "The fans have been unbelievable with me from day one and the club provides absolutely everything for its players.

"It is the best club in the world to be at. I have felt so much love and respect during my three years here, and I don't take that for granted.

"The players we have here are amazing. This is a world-class squad that is young and full of potential.

"I truly believe we will have a lot of success in the coming years."

Director of football Hugo Viana added: "He epitomises what we want in our defenders. He can play in multiple positions, he is quick and strong, and when he attacks he does it superbly.

"He is exceptional, but the way he conducts himself is also very impressive. This young man is determined to be the best he can be - an approach totally aligned with our overall vision."

title: Why Marlins manager Clayton McCullough compared team’s 12-game losing streak to ‘The Odyssey’
description: The Marlins' odyssey is over for now, in the eyes of manager Clayton McCullough.
fullText:
Why Marlins manager Clayton McCullough compared team’s 12-game losing streak to ‘The Odyssey’ originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The Marlins were one of the biggest surprises in baseball, until they weren't.

Miami went from 10 games under .500 and in playoff position to under .500 in an instant, losing 12 consecutive games after a dominant June. For manager Clayton McCullough, the journey was a reflection of one taken by Matt Damon.

McCullough compared his experience during the team's losing streak to that of Odysseus in "The Odyssey," taking a lighthearted approach before the Marlins snapped the skid with a comeback win over the Phillies on Monday.

Here's a look at why McCullough compared the Marlins' losing streak to "The Odyssey."

MORE:16 players who could be traded by MLB deadline

McCullough told reporters he recently saw "The Odyssey" in theaters on an off day and found that Odysseus' journey mirrors his own in some ways.

"I feel a bit like Odysseus," McCullough said. "Like I'm away from home for 10 years. At some point, I'm going to return home. I don't know what baseball god I infuriated, but it's where we're at, so today is an opportunity."

"Home," in this case, is the win column, and it's where McCullough and the Marlins returned on Monday when they overcame a ninth-inning deficit to walk-off the Phillies.

Christopher Nolan might disagree that what the Marlins have been through directly mirrors what Odysseus endured during an arduous decade-long journey. Then again, McCullough had to watch his team lose 11 of those 12 games by three runs or fewer, six of which they led at some point. Odysseus couldn't say the same.

MORE:Why the Tigers should (and shouldn't) trade Tarik Skubal

The Marlins were the talk of baseball after a terrific month of June, at one point reaching 10 games over .500 and moving into postseason position, but the wheels have fallen off in July.

Miami was swept by the Guardians going into the All-Star break and couldn't get out of that rut in the three series that followed, suffering sweeps at the hands of the Brewers, Astros and Padres. Most games were close — the Marlins only lost by more than three runs only once in that span, but their bullpen struggled to hold leads and their offense grinded to a halt.

After seeing an early 5-2 lead slip away against the Phillies, it looked like the streak would be extended to 13. The Marlins instead rallied to load the bases with no outs and won after RBI singles by Heriberto Hernandez and Griffin Conine.

GRIFFIN CONINE. BALLGAME. pic.twitter.com/tHJCmfZILU

— Miami Marlins (@Marlins) July 28, 2026

Just like that, McCullough's long odyssey is over. The Marlins have plans to add on.

"As far as what this does, pressure's off," Conine said after his walk-off hit. "Now, we're on a winning streak. Now, we want more of it. So it's like forget the last two weeks and move on. I think we can learn from it, and I think that we will."

McCullough told reporters everyone in the clubhouse is "feeling much different" than they did before the game and said winning the series is the team's next goal.

Because the Diamondbacks lost Monday, the Marlins only find themselves two games out of a wild-card spot in the National League and could try to make another push after a report that they don't plan to trade any of their core pieces at the deadline.

title: Porsche Penske reveals retro liveries for IMSA’s Road America enduro
description: Two iconic liveries from different eras will return as Road America hosts IMSA’s fourth endurance race of the season
fullText:
Porsche Penske Motorsport will contest this weekend’s IMSA SportsCar Championship event at Road America in two special retro liveries.

The #6 Porsche 963 LMDh shared by Kevin Estre and Laurens Vanthoor will carry the blue-and-yellow Sunoco colour scheme made famous by the Porsche 917/30 in the 1970s.

Meanwhile, Julien Andlauer and Felipe Nasr will revive the bright yellow livery of the Porsche RS Spyder LMP2 when they take to the track in the #7 Porsche 963.

It marks the fourth time Porsche Penske has run special designs on its LMDh prototypes this season, having previously unveiled traditional liveries at Sebring, Long Beach and Laguna Seca.

2026 is a landmark year for the two brands. Porsche is celebrating its 75th anniversary in motorsport, while Roger Penske’s eponymous team was founded 60 years ago.

With the Road America round extended to six hours from the usual two hours and 40 minutes, Porsche and Penske have chosen the event to pay tribute to two of the most successful cars in their shared history.

“Road America has been the scene of special successes in the shared history of Porsche and Penske,” says Thomas Laudenbach, vice president of Porsche Motorsport.

“In 1973, the Porsche 917/30 dominated the scene. During qualifying, Mark Donohue became the first driver on this track to break the two-minute lap time barrier. Starting in 2006, the RS Spyder marked Porsche’s return to prototype racing across several championships.

"I personally remember the success of 2007: I was there when Timo Bernhard and Romain Dumas drove to overall victory against the nominally more powerful LMP1 race cars.”

Roger Penske, founder and chairman of Penske Corporation, added: “Sportscar competition has been the foundation of Team Penske since the very beginning. As we continue to celebrate our team’s 60 years in motorsports alongside 75 years of Porsche Motorsport in 2026, we are excited to honour the heritage and legacy of both organisations.

“These two iconic car liveries pay tribute to championship-winning eras, legendary cars and the people who helped build our success. Team Penske’s partnership with Porsche is one of the most successful and enduring relationships in racing, and we are proud to celebrate our winning tradition together.”

The Porsche 917/30 was the final evolution of the iconic 917 and was launched in 1973 to compete in the now-defunct Can-Am Series. The car dominated the championship, with Team Penske driver Donohue going unbeaten in the final six out of eight races. The American also beat the field by three seconds in qualifying at Road America, making the 6.5km track a fitting venue to bring back the Sunoco livery.

Meanwhile, Porsche and Penske’s RS Spyder made a huge mark in LMP2 racing in the late noughties, claiming the LMP2 title in the American Le Mans Series for three consecutive years as well as two class wins at the Le Mans 24 Hours.

However, the car’s biggest achievement came in the 2008 Sebring 12 Hours, where Bernhard, Dumas and Emmanuel Collard beat the more powerful LMP1 prototypes to register the RS Spyder’s first overall win in the ALMS.

title: Rays draft tracker and signing board
description: Keeping track of the draftees joining the Rays organization
fullText:
The 2026 MLB draft has concluded!

Here we will be keeping track of each draftee taken by the Tampa Bay Rays over the course of the draft, their projected signing amount, and how much they actually signed for.

The Rays have a bonus pool of $19,09,300 that they are alloted to spend on the selections they made over the first 10 rounds of the draft; for every pick after the 10th round, any amount over $150,000 will be counted towards a team’s pool. 5-10%: 75% tax and lose future 1st round pick

10-15%: 100% tax and lose future 1st & 2nd round picks

15+%: 100% tax and lose two future 1st round picks

title: The FA confirm 3 new anti-timewasting rules
description: The FA have confirmed that the International Football Association Board have approved a new goalkeeper injury trial for the 2026/27 Premier League season.Photo by Michael Regan/Getty ImagesThe FA have...
fullText:
The FA have officially announced that English football has received approval from IFAB to trial a new system to cut down on tactical goalkeeper injury timeouts.

For a while, teams have abused the fact that a goalkeeper going down for medical treatment doesn’t have to leave the field of play afterwards. A goalkeeper can go down, disrupt momentum, and give their team time to address things tactically during the break, with no negative consequences.

The trial will introduce such a consequence, requiring the head coach to immediately nominate a player to leave the pitch for a minimum of one minute after the game restarts.

There will be exceptions to the rule, including if the goalkeeper is fouled, if the goalkeeper is bleeding, or if the goalkeeper and an outfield player have collided and both need attention.

But the hope is that this will cut down on potential sporting advantages associated with such stoppages.

The FA add that they will also be introducing a five-second countdown option for match officials to use when they believe players are unfairly delaying a throw-in or goal-kick. The system was used at the World Cup, and it will now be introduced in English football.

Finally, a ten-second limit will be in place for players leaving the pitch when substituted.

The trial will take place across the Premier League, the FA Cup, and the League Cup this season, as well as the upcoming Community Shield match. So it will apply to Arsenal in all competitions except the Champions League.

title: Why PSG might finally revive their interest in Leipzig’s Yan Diomandé?
description: Whilst Paris Saint-Germain appeared determined not to pursue their efforts to sign RB Leipzig’s Yan Diomandé (19), the arrival of new intermediaries – who are said to be much closer to the Rouge ...
fullText:
Whilst Paris Saint-Germain appeared determined not to pursue their efforts to sign RB Leipzig’s Yan Diomandé (19), the arrival of new intermediaries – who are said to be much closer to the Rouge et Bleu management – could well shake things up, according to reports in L’Équipe.

And this is particularly due to Real Madrid’s apparent difficulty in convincing their German counterparts to sell the Ivorian forward, even though the latter is said to have already reached an agreement to join the Spanish club. However, the expansion of his entourage in recent days is reported to have slowed down negotiations, whilst ever-increasing transfer fees are reportedly being demanded for the player.

This is a situation from which PSG could well benefit, as they are aware of Diomandé’s interest in their project and his strong desire to play under Luis Enrique. Whilst nothing is yet certain, the Parisians may nevertheless be tempted by the prospect of launching a final push in the coming hours – provided, that is, that Real Madrid do not manage to finalise the deal first.

title: The Most Important Packers: No. 1 — QB Jordan Love
description: Green Bay's Jordan Love has become one of the NFL's top quarterbacks, but is just 1-3 in the postseason.
fullText:
The Green Bay Packers were arguably the most disappointing team in football last year. And perhaps no one did less with more than Packers’ coach Matt LaFleur.

Green Bay headed into the 2025 season with one of the NFL’s top rosters, then traded for star defensive end Micah Parsons 10 days before the year began. Suddenly, Packer Nation was dreaming of their first Super Bowl appearance since 2010.

Instead, Green Bay went a remarkably unsatisfying 9-8-1 overall and was the NFC’s No. 7 seed for a third consecutive year. The Packers then blew a 21-3 halftime lead in the Wild Card round against Chicago, gave up 25 fourth quarter points and eventually suffered a shocking 31-27 loss to the arch-rival Bears.

“No way you should lose games in this league when you’re up that much,” running back Josh Jacobs said.

Green Bay, which began the year 9-3-1, finished the season with five straight losses. The Packers now enter 2026 with the league’s fourth-longest losing streak.

Collapsing late in games was the story of Green Bay’s 2025 campaign.

Green Bay had double digit leads in the final minutes twice against Chicago and also vs. Cleveland and somehow went 0-3 in those games. The Packers’ odds of losing all three contests were 1-in-250,000, yet they somehow did it.

“That (expletive), it’s starting to get damn-near embarrassing,” safety Javon Bullard said.

Rebounding won’t be easy as the Packers were hit hard in free agency and didn't have a first round draft pick.

Green Bay’s first training camp practice is July 29. Between now and then I will count down the ‘30 Most Important Packers’ heading into the 2026 campaign.

For the fourth straight year, quarterback Jordan Love is No. 1.

Love had arguably his finest season yet in 2025.

Love had a career-best passer rating of 101.2 that ranked No. 6 in the NFL. Love completed 291 of 439 passes (66.3%) for 3,381 yards and 23 touchdowns vs. just six interceptions.

Love’s interception percentage was just 1.4% and his touchdown-to-interception ratio was 3.83-1.

Love finished eighth in the league in yards per attempt (7.70) and tied for eighth in explosive passes (16-plus yards) with 81.

When teams blitzed Love, it usually backfired as he posted a 109.5 passer rating against the blitz that ranked fifth in the league.

And while the Packers’ playoff loss to Chicago is one of the more forgettable nights in team history, Love did all he could to lead Green Bay to victory. Love threw four touchdowns, no interceptions and posted a 103.8 passer rating that night in Chicago.

Love, a controversial first round draft pick in 2020, sat for three years behind Hall of Famer Aaron Rodgers. Then, when Love got his chance to take over in 2023, he made the most of it.

From 2023-25, Love ranks sixth in the league with 80 touchdowns. He’s also No. 8 in passing yards (10,929) and yards per attempt (7.57).

Love made all 19 starts in 2023, threw 37 touchdown passes and just 13 interceptions. During a two-month window between Week 11 and Green Bay’s NFC divisional playoff game at San Francisco, Love threw a remarkable 23 touchdowns and just one interception.

That’s something Green Bay legends Bart Starr, Brett Favre and Aaron Rodgers never did.

Love completed 409 of 634 passes (64.5%) for 4,625 yards and finished with a 98.5 passer rating in 2023. Love ranked second in the league in TD passes and seventh in total passing yards (4,159) that season.

Love signed a four-year, $220 million contract during training camp in 2024, then had an up and down second season as Green Bay’s starter.

Love suffered a sprained medial collateral ligament in the Packers’ Week 1 loss to Philadelphia and missed the next two games. He later missed half of a Week 8 game at Jacksonville with a groin injury and three quarters of a Week 18 loss to Chicago with a right elbow injury.

Despite those injuries, Love threw 25 TDs, 11 interceptions and had a 96.7 passer rating. Love ranked 19th in the league passing yards (3,389) and completed 63.1% of his passes.

Love had a passer rating of at least 107.7 in five straight games between Weeks 11-15, but was at 92.0, or less, the last four contests.

Love then threw three interceptions in Green Bay’s loss to Philadelphia in the NFC Wild Card game and had a season-low passer rating of 41.5.

When the season ended, many suggested Love had regressed in his second season as a starter.

“I mean, what is a step back is what I’d ask?” Love said when asked if he regressed in 2024. “Everybody has different opinions, things like that. You got to block that stuff out.”

Love, who will turn 28 in November, has done his part in carrying on the tremendous quarterback tradition in Green Bay.

He can make every throw. He’s as cool as January night in Green Bay. He’s become more of a vocal leader and he’s highly regarded by his teammates.

Now, the No. 1 question around Love is can he take the Packers on a deep playoff run?

Love won his first playoff game in 2023, but has lost his last three.

Fair or not, players are judged by what they do in the postseason.

There are 35 quarterbacks that have won a Super Bowl. Fifteen are in the Hall of Fame and eight others are locks or likely entrees when they become eligible (Tom Brady, Patrick Mahomes, Drew Brees, Ben Roethlisberger, Aaron Rodgers, Matthew Stafford, Eli Manning and Russell Wilson).

Love has all the tools to become one of the NFL’s elite quarterbacks, but needs to lead Green Bay deep into the playoffs for that narrative to develop.

“Jordan's been awesome, man. Like every year, he just continues to grow as a leader, you know. His consistency is remarkable. Who he is on a daily basis, showing up, how he works, how he leads others, he's pulling guys with them. So I'm really excited about what, you know, is in store for him.” — Packers coach Matt LaFleur on Love

“When I stepped away, it was just two seasons with him, right, so a pretty big difference in maturity, of the command of the offense and also, so it was a quite a few years difference there. But it was just a lot of fun when I step back in it and got to see him really running the show and him in complete control and the comfortability. I think one of his best traits is just that his cool, calm, collected mentality, and then just seeing that match with all the high-level functionality of the mental part of the game. It was really cool to see that when I got back – just a natural growth for his game.” — Packers quarterbacks coach Luke Getsy on Love

“For me, my biggest thing that I’ve noticed since I got back is just my feet in the pocket, trying to be as smooth and consistent as possible. When I go through my reads, get into my hitches and not getting antsy, not getting to that point where you’re trying to move through the pocket too fast. Just staying calm, staying relaxed, move through my reads.” — Love on what he focused on this offseason

This article was originally published on Forbes.com

title: Real Madrid summer signing trains under Mourinho for the first time
description: Denzel Dumfries has officially begun his Real Madrid career after reporting to Valdebebas on Tuesday morning for his medical examination and training.The 30-year-old right-back, one of the club’s su...
fullText:
Denzel Dumfries has officially begun his Real Madrid career after reporting to Valdebebas on Tuesday morning for his medical examination and training.

The 30-year-old right-back, one of the club’s summer signings, completed the routine medical tests at the Sanitas Clinic before joining Jose Mourinho’s squad for training later in the day.

In doing so, Dumfries becomes the first summer signing to begin pre-season training for Real Madrid.

Following his medical check-up, Dumfries started in the gym before moving onto the pitch to perform various running drills and ball exercises under the watchful eye of the new manager.

Dumfries has now ended his summer break following the Netherlands’ elimination from the 2026 FIFA World Cup, where they were knocked out by Morocco in the Round of 16.

The Dutch international joins Real Madrid after the club activated his €20 million release clause to sign him from Inter Milan.

His arrival strengthens the right side of the Merengues’ defence following Dani Carvajal’s departure earlier this summer.

After arriving at Valdebebas early on Tuesday morning, Dumfries met his new teammates and had the opportunity to speak with Mourinho for the first time since completing his move.

As things stand, however, Dumfries is not expected to feature in Real Madrid’s behind-closed-doors training match against Leganes later today.

But it is likely that he is present in the stands at the Alfredo Di Stefano Stadium to watch his new teammates in action.

As things stand, Trent Alexander-Arnold is ahead in the pecking order of things at right-back for Real Madrid, having been present for pre-season under Mourinho from the first day.

But, Dumfries is a player that the Portuguese tactician specifically requested and fits more with his style of play.

The experienced defender also arrives on the back of a title-winning season with Inter Milan in Serie A, which was followed by a strong run of displays at the World Cup despite his team’s underwhelming overall performance.

So, it will be interesting to see how things develop and who starts the new campaign as Mourinho’s preferred choice at right-back for Real Madrid.

title: 47 days till Arizona Cardinals' opener: Remembering the 1947 season
description: With 47 days until the Arizona Cardinals' 2026 opener, let's look back at their 1947 season.
fullText:
We continue the countdown to the start of the Arizona Cardinals' regular season. Today, Tuesday, July 28, is 47 days away from the Arizona Cardinals' regular-season opener on Sept. 13 on the road against the Los Angeles Chargers.

With 47 days until Week 1, let's look back at the 1947 season for the Cardinals.

The Cardinals have never won a Super Bowl, but they won the NFL Championship in 1947. They went 9-3 in the regular season and then beat the Philadelphia Eagles 28-21 in the championship game.

Running back Elmer Angsman had two 70-yard touchdown runs, running back Charley Trippi had a 44-yard touchdown run and a 75-yard punt return for a touchdown. Paul Christman only completed three passes in 14 attempts and was picked off twice, but the Cardinals rushed for 282 yards to be crowned champions.

Receiver Mal Kutner and guard Buster Ramsey were both second-team All-Pros in 1947.

Christman led the Cardinals with 2,191 passing yards, 17 touchdown passes and 22 interceptions.

Angsman's 412 rushing yards and seven touchdown runs, while Trippi, a rookie in 1947, rushed for 401 yards and two scores, and he had 23 catches for 240 yards.

Pat Harder rushed for 371 yards and seven scores.

Kutner had 43 receptions and led the NFL with 943 yards. He scored seven times.

Red Cochran's eight defensive interceptions led the team.

Harder made a league-high seven field goals.

title: PSG winger Bradley Barcola reaches agreement in principle to join Liverpool

fullText:
Paris Saint-Germain’s Bradley Barcola (23) is reported to have reached an agreement in principle to join Liverpool, according to information from L’Équipe.

Having made it clear to his club’s management that he does not wish to extend his contract – which runs until 2028 – with Les Rouge et Bleu, the French winger is said to have recently spoken with the Reds’ new manager, Andoni Iraola, to discuss a potential move.

Although they are far from having reached an agreement on the terms of a transfer at this stage, Liverpool and PSG are indeed in talks to find common ground. The outcome of the deal could hinge on a fee in excess of €120m.

At 23, and after three successful years in the French capital, Barcola is now keen to take his career to the next level and establish himself as a potential first-team regular at a major European club. Often relegated to the role of 12th man in PSG’s key fixtures in recent months, the Lyon-born player now seems determined to spread his wings, having reportedly identified Anfield as his preferred destination should a transfer go ahead.

title: 'Only job I wanted': France turn to Zidane as coach
description: Zinedine Zidane was appointed France coach on Tuesday, as widely expected, following the departure of Didier Deschamps, the French Football Federation (FFF) announced."The France job was the only one I wanted," Zidane said at his unveiling in Paris, where he signed autographs and took photos with fans waiting outside the FFF headquarters after his appointment.
fullText:
Zinedine Zidane was appointed France coach on Tuesday, as widely expected, following the departure of Didier Deschamps, the French Football Federation (FFF) announced.

Zidane, 54, had long been viewed as the leading candidate for the role and had been waiting for an opportunity to take charge of the national team for several years.

He will replace Deschamps, whose tenure began in 2012 and ended earlier this month after France finished fourth at the World Cup.

Deschamps guided France to 2018 World Cup glory and the final four years later.

"For me, it's an immense joy... being able to become the coach of this French team. I don't have any other words," said Zidane, who takes over on a four-year deal that runs until the 2030 World Cup co-hosted by Spain, Portugal and Morocco.

"I'm holding myself back because I have so many emotions inside me. I'm ready for the challenge, that's what drives me today."

Former Real Madrid star Zidane, who was Deschamps' teammate in the 1998 World Cup triumph, has been readying himself for the role since leaving Real Madrid in 2021.

"The France job was the only one I wanted," Zidane said at his unveiling in Paris, where he signed autographs and took photos with fans waiting outside the FFF headquarters after his appointment.

"I've had offers over these four or five years to take charge of a club and I turned them all down for the French national team."

The former France playmaker, who scored twice in the 1998 World Cup final victory over Brazil and also won the 2000 European Championship as a player, has coached only one club, Real Madrid.

During his time with the Spanish giants, he led them to three consecutive Champions League titles in 2016, 2017 and 2018, an unprecedented achievement in the competition's modern era.

"I think it's a completely different job, that's for sure," said Zidane. "I've experienced the club side of it. Now this is something new for me, but it doesn't scare me."

Zidane will follow in the footsteps of former international team-mates Laurent Blanc, who coached the national side from 2010 to 2012, and Deschamps.

"I'm going to give everything so that this team keeps on winning. That's it, the only thing that drives me is being able to work for this France team and making sure it keeps on winning."

"'DD' (Deschamps) is 'DD', Blanc was Blanc and 'Zizou' is Zizou'.

"I will do things the way I know how to do them."

FFF president Philippe Diallo said he first met with Zidane in February 2025, shortly after Deschamps revealed he would step down from his role after the 2026 World Cup.

"There was one thing that struck me, that perhaps ultimately made the difference," said Diallo. "During the conversations we had, he said to me, 'President, I know how to win.'

"When he said that, I saw someone who had both the desire and the self-belief needed to lead France. That is what it takes for our national team to remain successful in the years ahead."

Zidane's first game at the helm of France will come away to Turkey in the UEFA Nations League on September 25. His first match at home will be against Italy at the Stade de France on October 2.

France captain Kylian Mbappe and all-time leading scorer welcomed the arrival of Zidane, posting a message that read "Welcome home" on Instagram.

Mbappe became the first player to win the World Cup Golden Boot twice after scoring 10 goals at this summer's tournament.

title: The GOP’s New Red Scare
description: Chris...
fullText:
McCarthyism, the second time as farce.

Shortly after announcing the mission of turning the 2026 midterms into a “hate election,” the campaign brain trust for the Republican Party has settled on the secret-weapon epithet it plans to deploy against its Democratic congressional rivals: “Communism.”

No, really: Three and a half decades after the collapse of the Cold War, the campaign chieftains of the right are planning to revive the paranoid political stylings of Joe McCarthy. The rationale for this round of 21st-century red-baiting stems largely from the recent string of primary wins racked up by Democratic candidates aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America; in the perfervid imaginings of the right, socialists are just genteel stalking horses for Communists, with Marxism serving as the intoxicant of choice for raving leftists of all description. So the thing to do is to call out any and all Democrats as no-good Reds, determined to undermine and overthrow true-blue American individualism and laissez-faire capitalism at every term.

This advice is distilled in a polling memo that the conservative political research firm co/efficient drafted for the House Republican Conference and circulated to GOP House members on July 20. Washington Examiner reporter Hailey Bullis obtained the document, which peddles this spittle-flecked counsel to GOP House candidates: “Call them what they are: Socialists, Marxists, Communists. Communism rings the loudest alarm with constituents (42 percent name it the most dangerous system).… Connect all three, fruit of the same poisonous tree, and let the family name carry the alarm.”

There are a few difficulties with this line of argument, to put it mildly. To begin with, of course, Communism was never anything more than a fringe-minority allegiance in American politics, even during its heyday in the “Red decade” of the 1930s. The penchant for descrying it as a lurking menace in—take your pick—American university classrooms, federal government bureaucracies, diplomatic redoubts, labor unions, and the liberal intelligentsia typically said more about the persecution complexes raging through the id of the American right than it did about the actually existing state of recruitment activities by an American Communist Party that claimed membership in the tens of thousands at its peak. That became the damning consensus view in the wake of the alcoholic and demented McCarthy’s self-implosion on the national stage three years prior to his death.

Yet the primal grievances of the American right are endlessly fungible, and can be repurposed with just a few minor linguistic tweaks or revamped Kulturkampf come-ons. The revival of McCarthyite insinuations and smears is a convenient conceit for a MAGA movement that’s losing any plausible footing in public opinion, thanks to the Trump administration’s pointless and epically unpopular war in Iran and singularly maladroit management of the economy. (The Trump administration’s staggering corruption is also starting to make a noticeable dent as a campaign issue, despite the Democrats’ stupefying inability to make it an election-year crusade.) The GOP’s lurch into red-baiting is the electoral version of the old lawyer’s saw: “If you have the facts on your side, pound the facts. If you have the law on your side, pound the law. If you have neither the facts nor the law, pound the table.”

Then there’s the opinion survey that the co/efficient campaign savants treat as gospel. On the face of things, it’s monumentally incoherent. Start with the poll’s top-line finding that “63 percent of Americans are very or somewhat concerned about socialist candidates taking office.” On inspection, none of the poll’s lead respondents—who are clustered into numbingly broad categories such as “women” and “Americans of color” that disclose almost no useful information about their actual demographic profiles or broader political worldviews—clock majorities in the “very concerned” affiliation, while the “somewhat concerned” designation is so pointedly nonsignifying that Susan Collins has forged an entire political career out of it. It’s reasonable to infer that this 63 percent bloc represents the largely unformed views of voters just tuning into a primary cycle that’s been awash in centrist and right-wing freakouts in the elite media about the alleged specter of a DSA takeover of the Democratic Party. One useful corrective to such frantic hand-waving is this sturdy data point: The most prominent democratic socialists now holding office are among the most popular politicians in the country.

Now consider the findings that prompted these polling wizards to tie up all Democratic candidates in a tidy red bundle. The query to respondents was: “What do you consider the most dangerous system of government for the United States to pursue?”—not exactly a phrasing designed to yield much in the way of thought or reflective nuance. The offered range of response is a further case study in preselected bias: Communism (42 percent), socialism (15 percent), Marxism (6 percent).

That’s it: the whole spectrum of co/efficient-branded government danger. No mention of rampant authoritarianism or fascism, Christian nationalism, tech oligarchy, or Muskism—all far more present threats to the well-being of ordinary American voters, and many of which are polling worse than the Communist specter is among voters. Indeed, a reality check to all this brackish electoral Bircherism is a recent poll conducted by the anything-but-pinko news outlet CNBC finding that voters would prefer a DSA candidate over one endorsed by President Donald Trump or (worst of all) one strongly identified with the MAGA movement. Another reality check comes from a recent Economist/YouGov poll on the communism question, which found that just 18 percent of respondents regarded the moribund ideology as a major threat on the American scene; 25 percent designated the threat level as “minor,” while a 33 percent plurality declared it, on the soundest empirical grounds, not a threat at all.

And here, too, the survey’s historical incoherence is a wonder to behold. To throw the disparate forces of Communism, socialism, and Marxism all together as “fruit of the same poisoned tree” in a decidedly post-Communist global order is akin to ascribing the onset of the Industrial Revolution to the distempers of Greek mythology. In all likelihood, Communism carried the day among the poll’s harangued respondents as a simple exercise in name recognition: It’s the ideology that Americans have been most forcefully instructed to despise for more than a century, whereas socialism has produced many central and tangible improvements to the fortunes of working Americans. The 6 percent of respondents who went out of their way to calumniate Marxism are the rough polling equivalent of a shrug emoji. (It also says everything about the methodology here that Marxism is not a system of government at all but a nearly 200-year-old philosophy; socialism antedates it by about another century—unless, that is, you count the early Christians.)

Still, it’s clear that the red-baiting branding will continue apace on the right as it tries to seize on any and every brand of grievance calculated to distract attention away from its actual governing record. In a July 3 speech at Mt. Rushmore, Trump declared that the “communist menace” is once more stalking the American civitas, and vowed to “vanquish Communism quickly” and send its adherents “into exile.” He also vowed to continue the MAGA purge of dissent from universities and public discourse—a stance his administration is now planning to codify into a series of ideological disclaimers slapped on to American-history installations at the Smithsonian and elsewhere: “As for those who peddle Marxist lies about our heritage, tell our children that we live on stolen land or that our heroes were oppressors, they’re doing something much worse than slandering our past. They are slandering and attacking our future—not going to let that happen.” Trump’s State Department followed up that outburst with a high-paranoid report on the alleged global red threat called “Cuba: the Capital of Twenty-First Century Communism,” which delivered this fantasia of Castroite world dominance: “For nearly seven decades, the Cuban regime has waged a sustained campaign of subversion against the United States.… Today, that network continues to maintain ties to powerful leftist nonprofits, anti-ICE collectives, socialist groups, and Marxist militant organizations across the United States.”

Even during the many derangements of the Cold War, such unhinged conspiracy-mongering was chiefly fodder for public derision and satire. It’s now the everyday discourse of our presidency and State Department—a twist that poor drunken Joe McCarthy could never have envisioned, but that was always plainly in the sights of his far more disciplined lieutenant Roy Cohn, who also doubled as Donald Trump’s political mentor. Yet what neither Trump nor his quisling party seem to understand is that Cohn never had a chance in hell of being elected to anything. Good luck running on his platform in 2026.

title: Bee Gees at the bowls as Scotland para mixed pairs retain Commonwealth gold
description: Scotland defended their gold medal in the bowls para mixed pairs B2-B3, beating England to the tune of the Bee Gees.
fullText:
In hall three at the SEC Centre, the Bee Gees were telling us we should be dancing before 9am.

It wasn't some early morning disco, but instead the venue for the para mixed pairs B2-B3 final.

This Commonwealth Games has lamped a real focus on inclusiveness. Few sports are more inclusive than bowls.

And with this new format - two five-end sets - plus the addition of a DJ and a big glitter ball, bowls is trying to captivate a new audience.

Those boogieing along to the beat early on Tuesday were treated to a highly-competitive, nail-biting showdown between Scotland and England, with the Scots winning after a tie-breaker.

Skip Robert Barr and his director Sarah Jane Ewing won this title at an "exceptional" Birmingham four years ago, but this time, in front of a home crowd with lead Mary Stevenson and her director Jim Aitken, back-to-back gold medallist Barr said "this was just even better".

Glasgow roars for new Scottish heroes as Sandilands & Bryce claim glory

'Medal dream didn't come true but my other dream is fighting brain cancer'

MacInnes overcomes nerves to win swimming silver

What was also better for Barr was he didn't even need to deliver his final bowl.

After forcing the one-end shootout by taking the second set, Scotland opted to take the last bowl, rather than going first and taking the jack, after winning the coin toss.

The marker had to ask a nearby photographer for the coin, and though he dug deep into his pocket to find a dime, the Scots dug even deeper.

England lead - the country's oldest athlete at these Games - Ron Homer drew a beauty to within inches of the jack, forcing Barr to batter it out with his first bowl of three.

Visually-impaired, the players are often seen whipping out their telescopes to take in their effort. There was no need here for Barr. Bosh. Job done... for now.

Skip Sally-Ann Lewis-Wall resplendently replaced it. England lie for gold. Back to you, Robert.

This time, his hit was not so accurate, but after a run of rotten luck and near misses during the match, he got a wee rub off a high bowl, redirecting his pacy effort to pick up the jack and send it straight on to a gratefully awaiting blue bowl.

Gold medal back in Scotland's hands with just one England bowl remaining. Talk about tense.

As difficult a shot as they come, Lewis-Wall couldn't produce any more magic as the Scottish quartet were jumping in a huddle with the crowd bawling and showering themselves in Saltires.

An 08:30 kick-off for a final is far from ideal, but it didn't deter the swarms of spectators packing in to take in the action.

The home crowd came with high hopes, not only because of their status as defending champions, but for the group campaign and semi-final performance the team have put on in Glasgow.

The players felt that pressure but they dealt with it comfortably.

"I'm really delighted for Mary and Robert," Aitken said. "They've played fantastic all week and they've kept really calm under a lot of stress and a lot of expectation.

"They've been absolutely fantastic."

Ewing, who stands on the podium alongside Barr again admitted she "could greet" at the pride in the players alongside her, as they continue to break the stigma of the sport being an old man's game.

Beside me in the media tribune, one of Team England's media members - and bowls first-timer - told me how she felt more patriotic watching this, than the football World Cup a matter of weeks ago.

She was hooked. And sticking around for the rest of the day's action.

A win for Scotland, a win for the sport.

title: Shootouts & regional fixture split for new-look League Cup
description: The Players Cup, formerly the League Cup, will have a 23-team league phase that includes penalty shootouts to settle draws after 90 minutes.
fullText:
The Women's League Cup will be renamed the Players Cup and operate in a league system with regionalised matches for the 2026-27 season.

Last November, clubs in the Women's Super League (WSL) and WSL 2 voted in favour of proposals to revamp the competition to help combat scheduling issues and to protect player welfare.

They agreed the new format would exclude sides who have qualified for the Women's Champions League, meaning League Cup holders Chelsea, WSL champions Manchester City and runners-up Arsenal will miss this year's edition.

The remaining 23 teams from the top two divisions have been split into Northern and Southern sections - but will be in one table.

They will compete from September to December on nights when Champions League fixtures are taking place.

Each team will play three home and three away games against sides in their region, with three points for a win.

Any match that is level after normal time will be decided by a penalty shootout, with the victor gaining two points and the loser awarded one.

The top eight will qualify for the quarter-finals in January, when higher-placed finishers will be granted home advantage.

After a one-legged semi-final hosted by the higher seed, the final will be scheduled at a neutral venue on the weekend of 13 and 14 March.

"We wanted meaningful playing minutes for young and fringe players and to address disparity on playing opportunities across the leagues, without compromising our player welfare principles," WSL's chief revenue officer Zarah Al-Kudcy said.

Last season, teams played three or four matches across five groups, with the winners of each being joined at the quarter-final stage by sides in European competition.

Fixtures will be announced on Thursday, 6 August.

Northern section: Aston Villa, Birmingham City, Burnley, Durham, Everton, Liverpool, Manchester United, Newcastle, Nottingham Forest, Sheffield United, Sunderland.

Southern section: Brighton & Hove Albion, Bristol City, Charlton Athletic, Crystal Palace, Ipswich Town, Leicester City, London City Lionesses, Southampton, Tottenham Hotspur, Watford, West Ham United, Wolves.

Champions League teams set to miss Women's League Cup

Pressure on the football calendar is not unique to the women's game and when WSL Football was founded in late 2023, it recognised an opportunity to revamp the League Cup.

This new format comes out of consultation with clubs, players and fans to service the needs of all teams in the top two divisions.

There is a vast disparity between the number of fixtures played by those in European competition and those not - more than 10 in many cases last season.

Therefore, mirroring the Swiss-style format of the Champions League, the new Players Cup seeks to address that by providing more opportunity and minutes for players of those teams who did not finish in the top three of the WSL in 2025-26.

Similarly, not having those top sides parachuted into the competition at the quarter-final stage not only offers greater parity for different clubs to win silverware, it also guarantees a new name on the trophy in 2026-27.

Only Arsenal, Chelsea and Manchester City have ever won the League Cup - and as they are excluded this season, the Players Cup will have a first-time winner.

title: England keeper Hampton extends deal at Chelsea
description: England international Hannah Hampton signs a new two-year deal with Chelsea.
fullText:
England international Hannah Hampton has signed a new two-year deal with Chelsea.

The goalkeeper's contract was set to expire this summer and it was key that Chelsea kept her as part of an effort to bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 campaign.

After joining from Aston Villa in 2023, Hampton has become one of the world's best goalkeepers and cemented her position as first choice for the Lionesses.

The 25-year-old has won five trophies during her time in west London and was a standout performer as England won Euro 2025.

She won the Yashin Trophy for best goalkeeper at the Ballon d'Or awards last year and joins fellow England internationals Lucy Bronze and Aggie Beever-Jones in signing new Chelsea deals this summer.

"I'm really happy," Hampton said. "Chelsea have always been my dream club to play for in England so to be able to extend for another two years is a proud moment.

"When I moved to London from the Midlands, it was my first time moving away from home and everyone at Chelsea made it feel like a home away from home and somewhere I have been able to grow, not only as a player, but as a person.

"I don't want that journey to stop and I want to continue to grow more and learn more as a person. I know there is so much more I can achieve and so much more, we as a team, can achieve.

"I am going to do everything I can to help Chelsea get back to being as successful as we have been in the past."

Hampton was also part of the England squad that won Euro 2022 and reached the 2023 Women's World Cup final.

She helped Chelsea to an unbeaten domestic treble in 2024-25 and has claimed back-to-back Golden Glove awards in the WSL.

Chelsea have gone through a transitional year with several big-name players leaving this summer upon expiration of their contracts.

Striker Sam Kerr, midfielder Guro Reiten and former club captain Millie Bright all left at the end of the season, while several other players remained out of contract.

Hampton's renewal was vital for Chelsea's future plans and there was growing anxiety from the fanbase on whether an agreement had been reached.

She has had a difficult few years in the media, with the release of Mary Earps' autobiography throwing her into the spotlight, but Hampton's quality on the pitch has been clear.

Widely regarded as one of the most talented goalkeepers in the WSL, this season she will hope to reproduce the form she showed during Euro 2025.

title: Whiston wins Commonwealth gold after ill father makes rare trip
description: Para-swimmer Brock Whiston says she wanted to make her father Gel proud as he watched poolside for the first time in 17 years.
fullText:
Brock Whiston was already Paralympic champion, world champion and world record holder before these Commonwealth Games.

There were two things missing, however.

First, a Commonwealth gold medal. Second, it had been 17 years since her father Gel was poolside to watch her race.

"He doesn't like swimming," England's Whiston, 29, told the BBC.

"He finds it too hot - doesn't like the smell of chlorine."

The last time Gel came to watch was when Whiston's mother had cancer. She has since recovered.

Since then he has been a big "sideline supporter" from home - Whiston says he worked "so hard to get me to where I am today" - but has recently received a Parkinson's diagnosis.

This time he was keen to make the trip.

"I just wanted to make him proud," Whiston told TNT Sports.

"I just wanted to win this race for him. I didn't care about the time."

And win the race Whiston did - in a new Games record for the women's 100m breaststroke SB8.

This month Whiston, who works in a primary school, spoke about wanting to keep her emotions in check, having missed out on gold in the same event at the Paris Paralympics after being overawed by the crowd.

"I didn't spot him until I was doing my lap with my medal," Whiston said.

"He gave me a kiss on the head and said 'love you'. I think he was shellshocked."

So will he be back? Whiston's Games in Glasgow are finished but there are more meets to come.

"He said he's done it now. He's not coming back," she said.

"He is very happy to support from home.

"Just to have him there that once was a special moment."

title: What is it like to be a second XI cricketer?
description: Sheridon Gumbs, who has just signed a deal with Leicestershire after 18 months on trial, reveals what life can be like as a second XI cricketer.
fullText:
Every ball counts. It is a slogan made for The Hundred competition - the pyrotechnic-charged, music-pumping version of cricket bankrolled by billionaires.

It is a world away from what you get on the fringes of the professional game, where first-class cricket meets well-manicured English village grounds that so often host second XI matches.

For some, playing for the 'twos' is a tightrope cricketing existence and a last shot at trying to make it as a professional. Every ball really could count.

But unlike The Hundred, where top earner Harry Brook will pocket £465,000 for a month's work, some second XI players on trial runs with County Championship sides are rocking up to play in matches on the UK daily minimum wage of just over £100, with a little more on top for expenses.

That's what it was like for Sheridon Gumbs as he toiled day-to-day, game-by-game trying to prove himself at Leicestershire during a trial period that spanned a season and a half.

For 18 months there was no contract, just that day rate, as the former Surrey youngster and England Under-19 international tried to piece together a career with a hit and hope attitude.

"You don't have that safety net because coaches are under no obligation to let you know how you're getting on or how you're sizing up to be part of that first team," the 22-year-old told BBC Sport.

"To me, it was go to training and if you're picked, rock up, try your best, try to perform and just take it and play it by ear.

"Yeah, 18 months is a long time, but you've just got to trust it.

"Nothing easy is worth having and it's professional sport - it's not meant to be easy. It's cut-throat.

"So if you really want it, then go out and get it. It's a gamble, I guess."

But there is a reason Gumbs stuck at it with the East Midlands side when rival County Championship clubs began to show interest in him – and why that gamble would eventually pay off.

It was just days before the lucrative Hundred competition started last week that Gumbs' willingness to persevere was rewarded with a three-and-a-half-year deal at Leicestershire.

"There were a lot of people last year that sort of said 'what's going on'? Gumbs recalled. "I was putting runs on the board, having a lot of success and people were like, 'oh, Leicestershire are messing you around, this, that and the other'.

"But I had nothing, I almost felt in debt to Leicestershire. They reached me out of this hole and granted me this opportunity."

A succession of setbacks as a teenager meant Gumbs almost gave up on his career before it ever really got going.

He was released by Surrey just months after returning from Australia where he played for the England Under-19 team in 2023.

A trial run at Hampshire followed - but ended after just a few matches.

And at that point, he even thought about dropping out of Loughborough University – the one place he wanted to study sports management because it is the home of the national cricket performance centre.

"I almost put cricket to bed after that, because at the back of my mind I was thinking, almost as an excuse, what more could I have done or shown?" Gumbs said.

"I obviously wasn't getting any sort of results anywhere.

"Cricket's a very mental sport and I think having that break and realising that I essentially owe it to myself to pursue it as a career and keep going, keep knocking on doors, has helped me in the long run."

Gumbs signs long-term Leicestershire contact

Listen to BBC Radio Leicester's Talking Foxes podcast

Gumbs' older brother Shelvin, an all-rounder that had trial spells with the second XI teams at Hampshire and Middlesex in the past, came up with much-needed encouragement at the time.

Crucially, he also helped get his sibling a shot with Leicestershire - with Foxes second XI coach Dips Patel being a former team-mate of Shelvin's at Loughborough Town.

"I won't be naive, I know I was very lucky with the opportunity that Dips granted me by contacting my brother because getting a chance of second XI cricket to start with is very hard," Gumbs said.

"There's got to be a gap in a team and you've almost got to have a bit of luck and be in the right place at the right time."

Gumbs grinned as he recalled the approach from Patel being a "kick in the bum" that helped him get "switched back on".

All the latest Leicestershire CCC news

Patel had watched Gumbs years earlier as a junior, training in the nets with his father Wilson, and had long tracked his career.

He knew what player he was potentially recruiting.

The challenge was getting Gumbs to stand out in what he freely admits can be a "manic" environment - where players on trial are thrust into a team alongside academy youngsters trying to pick their way up the ranks, and established County Championship players who may be in the second XI to regain fitness or form.

"There's a lot of emotions and there's a lot of different characters in that dressing room which you have to try to manage," Patel said.

"It can be a selfish environment because, in a sense, you are playing for someone's job aren't you?

"Every trialist that walks through the door will have players on tenterhooks and thinking 'oh my God, he could take my spot here'. And it's all right being under that pressure, because that is what professional sport is about.

"It's about giving them opportunities. You just have to be a coach and dad to everyone, and just be very straight with them."

And while Gumbs piled on the runs almost from the get-go, his is a story of persistence as much as potential - and Patel knows it.

"Sheridan is a rare story for the fact he stuck with it for so long," Patel said.

"I've seen lads like him, who come out of an academy and are playing for the second team, and then all of sudden they are not given a deal and they throw it all away.

"But it is understandable because they've got to go out into the world, earn money, and get a proper job."

Gumbs, whose only previous experience of first-team cricket came in a brief One-Day Cup spell with Surrey in 2022, finally got his chance to call cricket his job when handed a one-month deal with Leicestershire earlier this season.

He scored 49 in his second innings on his first-class debut for Leicestershire against Essex in June, then a week later he went on to play a part in the Foxes' milestone victory - their first in the top flight for 8,318 days - against Yorkshire.

While Gumbs' trial period may seem exceptionally long, it is not necessarily unusual - with Kashif Ali previously outlining he did "four or five years" of trials, external across a number of counties before establishing himself at Worcestershire.

Even Essex pace bowler Jamie Porter worked as a recruitment consultant, external while he played for the club's second XI when his early career stalled. And he has gone on to take 592 first-class wickets and counting across a 12-year career.

Patel does not hesitate when saying he sees a "15-year career" in Gumbs' future.

And Leicestershire director of cricket Claude Henderson and head coach Alfonso Thomas have invested in that possibility, handing the top-order batter a deal that will run until the winter of 2029.

Patel says Gumbs should no longer feel as if "he is walking on eggshells" when he now "has a job to do".

In recent years, the Professional Cricketers' Association (PCA) has worked with first-class counties to establish guidelines around the low-paid, high-stakes working environment that second XI trialists deal with.

Before 2021, there was no obligation for clubs to pay trialists when they featured.

Previously, the opportunity and hope that came from a game at that level was seen as enough.

An element of that still exists, with players not being paid for the first five days of a trial - which ensures not every chance taken to look at fresh talent has to be budgeted for.

Rich Hudson, PCA director of cricket operations, described second XI cricket as a "melting pot of different people, dynamics and tensions".

"You've got the pro trying to get himself back into form or come back from injury, and you've got the young kid in the academy who's desperately trying to prove he's worth a contract and learn his way and then there is the Sheridon-type player who is fighting for his life to get another contract and prove himself," Hudson said.

"We also understand the financial pressures of the game, which means that decision makers are constantly having to make calls that come with natural tension between doing what's right to support people in that environment and high-performance success, where the first team needs to be performing in the Championship and the T20 Blast."

And with Leicestershire's support, Gumbs says he is once again dreaming about what he can deliver as a cricketer.

"Making my Blast debut and just being in and around the lads, training in that sort of T20 environment, I 100% think there is going to be a push with my white-ball cricket and I want to see how far I go with that," he added.

"With the red ball, I want to wear the England badge again.

"My brother's always said, 'you're never that far away', but I've always thought on the flip side and almost thought, I'm miles away.

"This contract, and everything else that comes with it, is big and Leicestershire have granted me that sort of belief that maybe I'm not that far away whatsoever."

title: No excuses for Rangers as McInnes era is poised to begin
description: An experienced figurehead in the dugout, Lawrence Shankland spearheading the attack and further financial backing - there are few excuses for Rangers this season.
fullText:
The climactic end to the Scottish Premiership, coupled with the summer of football and managerial upheaval that followed, has made it somewhat easy to forget that Rangers finished last term third.

A lot has happened since head coach Danny Rohl, who has been replaced by Derek McInnes, watched his team limp to the finish after their season unravelled in a post-split collapse.

The memories of the Ibrox side's demanding fanbase are not that short, though.

They are expecting far better from a club that followed up a reported £40m spending spree with a second successive trophyless season.

But as the McInnes era prepares to kick into gear, are those same supporters heading into the new campaign with fewer reasons to fear more failure?

How many midfielders do Rangers need after busy summer?

Holders St Mirren visit Rangers in League Cup last 16

Who has your Premiership club brought in & let go this summer?

It was only a year ago that Russell Martin had just started his troublesome 17-match reign as Rangers head coach.

Now Leicester City boss, Martin was sacked after a brutal end to his brief spell. And after dragging the side back into the Premiership title fight before it all went wrong, Rohl too has been and gone, leaving for Red Bull Salzburg in June.

The nature of Rangers' end to last season - their hopes ending with four straight post-split defeats - meant Rohl would have been up against it with the fans on day one of the 2026-27 campaign.

Any credit the German had banked was diminished and a stuttering start to the new season would inevitably have led to the familiar social media meme poking fun at the vicious Rangers cycle once again reaching the managerial departure stage.

A "mutual agreement" that resulted in Rohl heading to Salzburg should help the Ibrox club avoid the recent trend of ripping everything up and starting again in the autumn, with McInnes tasked with taking the team forward.

Some have viewed the former Aberdeen boss, who turned down interest from Rangers in 2017, as a sensible appointment for years, while others have had doubts.

But taking Hearts to within about 10 minutes of a historic Scottish top-flight title went some way to unifying the view that the 55-year-old is now the right man.

"The timing's perfect," former Rangers midfielder Andy Halliday told BBC Scotland. "McInnes will probably admit himself he's now a more well-rounded manager than he was back in 2017.

"He's been through a title race, he's had ups and downs throughout that, so I think he's in the best possible place to take the job on. It's just a natural fit."

In Old Firm fan speak, boyhood Rangers fan McInnes 'gets it', having played at Ibrox from 1995 to 2000.

He won league and cup silverware during that spell but supporters will still harbour concerns about his ability to win big as a manager.

His only major honour across two decades in the dugout was the 2014 League Cup with Aberdeen, won on penalties after a goalless draw with Inverness Caledonian Thistle.

Only evidence will win over every doubter within Rangers' support, who have also lamented the lack of a figurehead during a tumultuous period of managerial upheaval.

Since Steven Gerrard's 2021 exit, appointments have been perceived by some more as project coaches but the Ibrox club have made it clear McInnes arrives as a manager, not a head coach.

A lack of leadership on the pitch has also come under scrutiny, with James Tavernier regularly the fall guy.

That criticism was arguably often unfair but the long-serving right-back departed this summer, vacating the captaincy and leaving a void to fill. Experienced goalkeeper Jack Butland has also left.

McInnes does not shy away from the fact he wants a Scottish core running through his squads and the arrivals of Lawrence Shankland and Ross McCrorie - also boyhood fans of the club - have strengthened the local contingent.

Rangers great Allan McGregor, who knows the club inside out, has also been brought back as goalkeeping coach.

Shankland, meanwhile, joins as a leader after captaining Hearts - as does former Sunderland skipper Dan Neil - but the Scotland striker also arrives as a seasoned Premiership scorer, having netted 88 goals in four years at Tynecastle.

Rangers fans and connected pundits had been crying out for the club to sign the striker long before he joined this summer.

Shrewd business has finally delivered the man the supporters have been desperate for to lead the line. Another box ticked?

"As a Rangers striker, hitting 20 goals should be the minimum," says Halliday, who played with Shankland at Hearts.

"If you look at the past few seasons, there have not been many Rangers number nines who have done that.

"If the service is there for Shankland, he's as close to a guarantee as you can possibly get to a 20-goal-a-season striker."

Halliday says McInnes "knows the pressure cooker he's stepping into". It will be like nothing he has experienced in the dugout previously.

Expectation may be high at Aberdeen and Hearts but the relentless need to win at the Old Firm is on another level.

As a former Rangers player who was brought up supporting the club, he will be aware of that, although he will still have to convince some fans that he has what it takes to drive the side back to consistently winning major honours.

An unknown quantity in Europe, having only managed in qualifiers, he will also have to navigate two ties to reach the Europa League proper, where Rangers have excelled in recent years.

But it is domestic pressure that his post-Gerrard predecessors have shown signs of struggling with, whether that has meant dragging the team into title fights and falling at the final hurdle or failing to mount a serious challenge.

On other occasions, the reality has been that they have been competing with a Celtic side boasting superior spending power and quality.

Following the takeover of the club by a US-based consortium, who now face a potentially defining season, the financial argument has quietened somewhat after a supposed £40m spend last season.

Despite the big backing, Martin immediately put himself on the back foot with an opening-day draw at Motherwell last August.

Twelve months earlier, Philippe Clement did likewise in the first match of his first full season in charge, drawing at Hearts. The year before that, Michael Beale lost at Kilmarnock.

A positive start in Friday's Premiership curtain-raiser at Dundee United is crucial for McInnes as excuses start to run dry.

Rangers play six league games before travelling to Celtic in the campaign's first Old Firm encounter. Halliday believes Rangers have to be flawless in each of them.

"There have been too many cases in the past where Rangers have gone into the first Old Firm of the season feeling they have to win," he adds.

"It's imperative they win every game in the lead up to it this year."

title: Former world champion Cordina denies assaulting man, court hears
description: Joe Cordina, 34, was charged in connection with an incident outside a petrol station in February.
fullText:
Former boxing world champion Joe Cordina has denied assaulting a man outside a petrol station, a court has heard.

Cordina, 34, was one of two men charged in connection with an incident in the Cardiff suburb of Pentwyn in February.

He appeared at Cardiff Magistrates' Court on Tuesday and pleaded not guilty to two charges of assault by beating.

Cordina appeared in the dock alongside Jamie O'Brien, 32, from Pentwyn, who has also been charged with assault in connection with the incident.

O'Brien did not enter a plea during the short hearing.

The court previously heard the offences the two men are charged with are alleged to be "against each other".

Nadeem Majid, representing Cordina, said the second charge of assault he faces "emanates from one continued incident".

District Judge Charlotte Murphy granted Cordina unconditional bail until a trial, which was set for 13 October this year.

O'Brien's case was adjourned until 26 August.

Cordina is a former super-featherweight world champion and was due to fight for the WBO lightweight title in the United States on July 4.

However, he revealed in a social media post that his application for a US visa was refused.

title: Rodri out for 'short period' after back surgery
description: Manchester City midfielder Rodri will be sidelined for a "short period of rehabilitation" following back surgery on Monday.
fullText:
Manchester City midfielder Rodri will be sidelined for a "short period of rehabilitation" following back surgery.

New manager Enzo Maresca said on Friday that Rodri would have an operation on Monday, and that he "needs a holiday, he needs to rest and recover and then he will be back with us".

No timeline has been set for his return.

City face Arsenal in the Community Shield on 16 August before their Premier League opener against Bournemouth on 23 August.

City said Rodri had been "feeling discomfort for some time but has now undergone a procedure to address the issue".

Rodri, who has a year left on his contract, has been heavily linked with a move to Real Madrid after guiding Spain to World Cup glory this month. He was named player of the tournament.

His past two seasons have been heavily disrupted by injury, and he missed most of City's 2024-25 campaign with a torn anterior cruciate ligament.

Meanwhile, as reported by BBC Sport in June, defender Josko Gvardiol has signed a new five-year deal which will keep him at the club until the summer of 2031.

The 24-year-old Croatia international has made 122 appearances for City since joining from RB Leipzig in August 2023, winning six trophies, including the Premier League in his debut campaign.

fullText:
PC, Nintendo Switch/Switch 2, PS5; SFB Games
Detective Grimoire is at it again in the long-awaited new entry to this stylish series of comedy whodunnits

In a boom time for mystery games, the Detective Grimoire series stands out for its style and sense of humour. The Mermaid Mask continues to build upon the formula laid down in Secret of the Swamp and polished in Tangle Tower, and while there is still room for further improvements this sequel is worth the seven years’ wait.

This time, the casually competent Grimoire and his smart if sarcastic sidekick Sally have been summoned to a submarine to solve the locked-room murder of its captain, Magnus Mortuga. You click around the cluttered rooms of the vessel to hear the detectives’ comedic commentary and look for clues and – closer up – click and drag to move objects around for further examination or to solve a puzzle. (For those playing on Nintendo Switch 2, the mouse controls are actually useful here, if not comfortable in the long run.)

Puzzles are never so taxing as to disrupt the flow: variations on “arrange these objects to satisfy some more-or-less apparent rules of logic” with stylistic wrapping. Your reward is generally an opened door and a new object to examine, which – importantly – you can then present to the various suspects.

And here is the chewy centre of these games: the fully voice-acted conversations with a cast of colourful characters. I immediately lowered the volume of the music (which sadly doesn’t compare to Tangle Tower’s characterful soundtrack) to better hear the well-performed dialogue. Some of the suspects are more memorable than others, but the somewhat supernatural backdrop (and these games are all set in very much the same world) allows for archetypes not found elsewhere.

Madam Tadpole is buff, green-skinned, and appears to have gills. Mariana Moon is an older woman with an unnaturally keen sense of smell whose voice acting is cleverly muffled when she’s chewing on her pipe. Godric Gripp is a compass repairman with an anthropomorphised stick called Cornelius Cane, whose introduction involves an unavoidable shopfront interface the developers must have coded purely for this one laugh.

These stylish moments are one of the more noticeable additions since Tangle Tower, with, for example, new 3D animations to illustrate the suspects’ recollections. But when it comes to solving the mysteries, they haven’t fixed what isn’t broken: as in Tangle Tower, and other deduction games such as the Golden Idol series and The Séance of Blake Manor, you form hypotheses by filling sentence blanks from a selection of nouns and verbs.

The overall process is soothingly methodical: your inventory shows blank slots for objects you’ve yet to find, each topic addressed with a suspect gets a satisfying tick, and Grimoire and Sally inform you when you’ve uncovered enough to tackle each suspect’s individual mystery (in one instance I did experience a bug where this unlocked prematurely, but the developers are already fixing bugs raised by early players).

Some players may find this completion percentage approach too formulaic, especially if they exhaust their current inventory and resort to pixel hunting to locate the rest. And the pacing does falter in the final chapter, where the game presents you with a more literal checklist to work through before you get to tie up each character’s loose ends and make your final accusation. But while the conclusion of The Mermaid Mask feels far more satisfying than that of Tangle Tower, these games are far more about the twisty journey and the laughs you have along the way.

The Mermaid Mask is out now; £17.75

title: Is struggling Ramsay-Peaty nearing the end?
description: Can Adam Ramsay-Peaty return to the top after a disappointing Commonwealth Games or is the end nigh for Britain's former Olympic champion?
fullText:
If you know what you are doing wrong, you can at least do something about it.

Adam Ramsay-Peaty, however, appeared at a loss after his second bronze medal of the Commonwealth Games.

"Nothing makes sense this week," the 31-year-old told BBC Sport.

Things that once came so easily – namely, speed and winning over one or two lengths of a swimming pool – now look out of reach.

So is this the end of the road for one of Britain's greatest Olympians, or can he turn the tide in time for the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028?

One thing Ramsay-Peaty, who went eight years unbeaten in the 100m from 2014 to 2022, did appear certain of was the need to change his training.

"I am working way too hard," he said. "I need to look at that."

Former freestyler Karen Pickering, who won her last Commonwealth title aged 30 in 2002, said she thinks Ramsay-Peaty "means is he is doing too much rather than too fast".

He has always been a brutally hard worker, one keen to push himself to his limits.

"I don't think more racing or training is the answer," Pickering said.

"More rest is understanding what your body needs - maybe not being around doing interviews at 11pm.

"It is learning to recover quicker. What do I need to eat? What do I need to drink? How do I get that lactic acid out of my body - massages or ice baths?

But Scottish former breaststroker Ross Murdoch, who was Ramsay-Peaty's first rival and spent much of his career racing and training with the Englishman, said: "I know Adam and he will find it hard to take his foot off the gas."

Even with a more bespoke training programme, Ramsay-Peaty cannot escape the hard facts.

Only six swimmers have won Olympic gold after their 30th birthday and only two – Americans Anthony Elvin and Dana Torres in 2016 and 2000 respectively – have done so aged over 33, the age Ramsay-Peaty will be during the LA Olympics.

When he returns to the pool in the European Championships next month he will face a stronger field than in Glasgow - one featuring Olympic champion Nicolo Martinenghi.

Ramsay-Peaty is also facing increasing pressure from Filip Nowacki, the 18-year-old from Jersey he mentors. Nowacki beat him to silver on Saturday and begins Wednesday's 200m event as favourite.

Still, Pickering says there are easy gains for Ramsay-Peaty to make as he attempts to get back to the top.

"He has never had a good start but I would say his starts here have been pretty average," she said.

"He doesn't seem to be deep enough in the water.

"Once he would swim a 50m breaststroke, give them a head start and win because he was swimming so fast. Maybe that hasn't been a priority.

"I would look at those skills and go back to basics. They are a relatively simple fix."

While Ramsay-Peaty has not found his best form in Glasgow and looks unlikely to touch his best times again, it would be wrong to say he has lost his pace altogether.

His time in the 100m breaststroke at the British Championships in April - 58.97 seconds - would have won Commonwealth gold.

His struggles have also come amid issues away from the pool.

He took a break from the sport in 2023 after issues with his mental health, and this week spoke of the "toll" external issues have taken.

When he married Holly Ramsay last year his parents were not present. He has had two different coaches since his long-time mentor Mel Marshall left for a job in Australia after the 2024 Olympics.

"Coming into the meet, he was vocal saying his priorities have changed, that winning isn't the most important thing in his life," Murdoch said.

"His young family will clearly be his priority, but the expectations of how the meet was going to go certainly haven't met the reality.

"In his heart of hearts did he really mean the swimming isn't the priority for him?

"I don't think that to be the case. I know Adam better than that. He will always want to fight and be the best he can be."

Ramsay-Peaty has said he wants to continue to LA.

He raised the prospect of racing only the 50m event in the future, given sprint events usually suit older athletes compared to the longer distances.

"Adam has always had a strong 50m," Murdoch said.

"At the start his skills were not what set him apart from everybody. It was his raw speed and power. That is the thing that really shone through.

"I don't believe that has gone. It is maybe the simple things that have gone away.

"I don't write him off on a 100 breaststroke. That raw speed will come back as your body recovers."

Pickering said: "[His pace] hasn't gone anywhere. He just couldn't access it.

"It is finding the best way to bring that out in an event like this.

"He should take some time to work through what has happened because it is a lot, but I wouldn't write him off."
