title: Spies in the sky: how worried should we be about the arrival of AI-enabled smart lamp-posts?
description:
The new breed of camera-equipped streetlights has the potential to fight crime and track down missing persons. Or will it just take Britain one step closer to a surveillance state?
How would you feel if your neighbourhood lamp-posts could recognise your number plate, and also your face? Maybe you wouldn’t mind, given how long we’ve had automatic number plate recognition and CCTV. What about if that lamp-post could power itself through its own solar panels, and perhaps find another use for any extra power generated – that would be good, right?
fullText:
The new breed of camera-equipped streetlights has the potential to fight crime and track down missing persons. Or will it just take Britain one step closer to a surveillance state?

How would you feel if your neighbourhood lamp-posts could recognise your number plate, and also your face? Maybe you wouldn’t mind, given how long we’ve had automatic number plate recognition and CCTV. What about if that lamp-post could power itself through its own solar panels, and perhaps find another use for any extra power generated – that would be good, right? This is what Conflow Power Group (CPG) in Warwickshire claims for its iLamps, the first of their kind in the UK.

What if lamp-posts had the potential to incorporate new AI capability – gait analysis, suspicious behaviours – that you haven’t even heard of? This is what the organisation Big Brother Watch worries about. And what if the home secretary had explicitly said she believed in a “panopticon state” – that is, a state that could watch you at all times (as Shabana Mahmood already has) – and what if she still had a job when the lamp-post eyes got their updates? Or what if the next home secretary was even keener on hyper-surveillance (hard to imagine), and the street apparatus was already in place? What about all the data this would harvest – who would own it?

It’s drizzling in Warwickshire, where I’m hoping to answer at least some of these questions in the hospital car park where some of these new “smart” lamp-posts have been installed. But if it wasn’t for me, nobody would probably be talking about them, not least because few have heard anything about them. Not many people know that the iLamp is not just solar-powered but can “double as a revenue-generating distributed AI datacentre”, according to CPG, let alone what that means. And nobody, not even me, knows how much of that potential functionality has been realised in the UK model – only what CPG has announced: that it has signed an agreement with the government of Katsina state, Nigeria, to supply it with 50,000 of these iLamps, which have additional surveillance potential for both vehicles and faces. CPG’s chairman, Edward Fitzpatrick, told the BBC World Service’s Tech Life programme that the lamp-posts could ultimately track down missing persons or fight crime, with the proviso that this would only be developed in partnership “with the relevant authority”.

CPG has been “extensively covered by worldwide media”, according to its own statement, and doesn’t take further questions, directing the media to its online material. As for the Warwickshire lamp-posts, the local authority directs all questions to the hospital, and the hospital doesn’t respond. Fair play – it’s a hospital.

A number of local residents have taken refuge from the rain in a bus shelter, most of them waiting for a partner to pick them up, and many are willing to chat. Karl, 52, who has been in a pub nearby, speaks for almost everyone when he says: “The town centre is already full of cameras, and it’s fine. You don’t mind them being there unless you’re up to no good.” No amount of loaded questions (What if you were doing something that was legal today but illegal in a year? What if the surveillance became predictive rather than reactive? What if you didn’t want anyone to know you’d been to the hospital? What if you weren’t supposed to be in a pub? Don’t you think you should at least have been asked whether you wanted it?) can separate anyone I speak to from the view that facial recognition is a tolerable part of life for a right-thinking citizen.

Tejal, 41, also waiting at the hospital bus stop, says: “I think we have to move on and accept that things change.” She’s a radiologist, and just seeing AI’s capability in her own sector makes her extremely anxious about AI as a whole. “I have anxieties for my children,” she says. That they won’t find entry-level jobs? “That, and that they’ll lose the ability to celebrate and find joy from the things we used to.” Privacy concerns do seem comparatively minor, compared with that.

Policy and technical experts are sceptical about some of the claims made for smart lamp-posts. Jasleen Chaggar, senior legal and policy officer at Big Brother Watch, says: “We see this quite often where local councils or other government agencies are … ‘swindled’ is a strong word, but they’re sold these tools as magic wands when there are limitations to what they can actually do.”

Prof Rabih Bashroush, director of the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Data Innovation at the University of East London, is blunt: “AI datacentres? There’s absolutely no chance this will fly: the technology doesn’t work, there’s not enough power, the economics won’t work …” Solar power to run the iLamps off-grid might work in Nigeria, but in Britain the amount generated by the lamp-posts is “negligible”, he says. You might be able to run an app that was “not mission critical, that you didn’t mind shutting down for a few days” – such as recognising whether a parking spot was occupied – but bigger claims for facial recognition are “just hype. Forget it – this has no legs.”

If he sounds impatient, it’s because he is: “It’s getting more and more difficult to get an independent opinion on things, because a lot of experts are in the industry now, and their view would have to align with their organisation,” he says. So a company might make a large claim, including a few AI buzzwords, ahead of a funding round; engineers don’t contradict them, local authorities don’t understand them and nobody else is even aware that anything has moved on since CCTV was invented.

Chaggar goes to great lengths to explain the conceptual difference between facial recognition and CCTV: “Facial recognition is not just passively recalling something, unlike CCTV, which you then check after the fact. What facial recognition does is real-time identity check: it’s much more like a fingerprint or DNA. It’s not like a passport – you can’t get another face.”

Another problem, Chaggar says, is that, “a lot of these technologies and infrastructures have capacity to add function later. Hammersmith and Fulham [in London] are updating their CCTV and it’s possible to embed facial recognition, monitor suspicious shopping behaviour, add aggression detection. So you can just turn the switch and it’s all there overnight.” A friend who lives in Fulham sent, by chance, a picture of a camera above a parking restrictions sign – it looks like a cross between Darth Vader and a beetle, and it whirrs as you go past, as if to indicate that it’s following your movements.

This throws up all the ageless privacy concerns, and it’s interesting how many people will wave away CCTV as a fact of modern life, but spontaneously raise how much they absolutely hate being listened to by their phone. Karl says: “I was talking to my mother the other day about dog nail clippers, and the advert came up on my phone that evening. I had my microphone off. I don’t even have a dog!” His friend Bob, 48, has ended up functionally off-grid, with no computer and a basic brick phone – a policymaker would probably describe him as “excluded” – simply because “some people like to be private”.

Another question about facial recognition software is: exactly how good are algorithms at detecting aggression and suspicious behaviour? “A lot of the software is pseudo-scientific,” Chaggar says. “So a company might try to sell emotion-detection, [claiming that] if people are walking through a train station, you can see if they’re angry or they’re about to be aggressive. There’s very little evidence to suggest that it’s accurate. If you’re a disabled person who moves differently, you might be flagged and have an intervention.” But the real question local authorities and any agents of the state should ask themselves, Chaggar says, is: “Are you happy to have your political enemies having these capabilities? Because you’re building an infrastructure that is here to stay.”

You can see that writ large in policing – the Home Office signed off on the use of facial recognition more than a decade ago, and the police have been “essentially using the public as guinea pigs for the past 10 years,” Chaggar says. What happens when the home secretary tells BBC 5 Live, as she did earlier this year, that “you can’t enjoy any of your liberties in any country if you’re not safe”? This sledgehammer logic, in which all liberties are secondary to the state’s rights as your protector, is chilling from a supposedly leftwing government. But the greater worry is that this doesn’t feel like the right time in politics to roll the dice on surveillance technology, basing our acceptance of it on the assumption that all future governments will be pro-social and democratic.

Wherever there’s potential to collect data, it throws up the question of who owns it: Bashroush used to work with the Internet of Things, the European Commission’s attempt to “connect the physical world to a digital environment”. “This was way back, before exiting Europe,” he remembers. “One of the challenges we saw was with a supplier [who was] basically collecting garbage from homes in the Netherlands, then optimising truck journeys and planning, based on your habits. The council that ran the programme was very happy with it, and tried to open the bidding a year later to get a more competitive price. The company said, ‘Sure, but the data is ours.’” That never got resolved: the contracts had been poorly constructed and the local authority lost the data.

If you want to see facial recognition go wrong without even any authoritarian intent or tech chicanery, you just have to look at the retail sector, where it’s already widely in use to prevent shoplifting. “We’ve seen misidentification by the police,” Chaggar says, “but in retail, when people are misidentified, it’s Kafkaesque. You’re just blacklisted from the store.”

And again, how much do people care, really? If you’re not allowed in a shop and you don’t know why; if a private company has a contract with your NHS trust, vaunting tech that isn’t operational yet and might never work, but nobody told, let alone asked, you; if the home secretary thinks it’s fine for the eyes of the state to be on you at all times – are these the building blocks of a dystopia, or do they just remind us how we used to describe dystopia, back before these surveillance capabilities existed?

The New Yorker essayist Ted Chiang wrote some time ago about the habit of projecting on to AI negatives that were actually not about tech but about economic systems, concluding: “Capitalism is the machine that will do whatever it takes to prevent us from turning it off.” Am I projecting on to AI and surveillance tech anxieties that are really about authoritarian politics?

“Well, if you haven’t got anything to hide,” says Sarah, 55, “I can’t see how it would be a problem. I’m presuming they’re actually lamps as well?”

title: AI sell-off intensifies as investors ditch chip stocks
description: Samsung and SK Hynix fall by more than 10% amid renewed fears over AI spending and Chinese...
fullText:
Samsung and SK Hynix fall by more than 10% amid renewed fears over AI spending and Chinese competition

The sell-off in AI stocks has intensified, driving South Korea’s stock market down to its lowest level in three months.

Investors continued to ditch chip stocks on Tuesday, amid rising concerns about the huge amount of borrowing among AI companies to fund their datacentre expansion plans.

The South Korean semiconductor companies SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics fell by more than 10%, dragging the country’s Kospi share index down by 11.5% to its lowest point since mid-April.

Analysts attributed the sell-off to renewed worries over AI investment spending, and competition from cheaper Chinese companies, after a report by the Information that China has begun mass production of homegrown deep ultraviolet (DUV) chip-making tools.

“We believe the market was likely spooked by the progress of China’s chip-making equipment capabilities, and was worried that this progress would threaten the competitive position of global chip making and chip equipment leaders,” said Jing Jie Yu, an equity analyst at Morningstar, adding that the sell-off was “largely a kneejerk reaction and overdone”.

On Monday, shares in the Chinese memory chip maker CXMT rose by 466% when it floated on the Shanghai stock exchange, underlining China’s drive to create its own AI supply chain.

Investors may also be growing jittery about the “circular funding” at the heart of the AI industry, through which artificial intelligence firms finance one another.

On Monday, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia was in discussions with OpenAI about providing $250bn (£188bn) for a massive datacentre project in Ohio. Backing from Nvidia, which has an investment grade credit rating, could make it less expensive to raise funding for the project.

News of the talks knocked Nvidia’s shares on Monday; they closed 5% lower, while the cost of insuring the chip company’s debt against default using a credit default swap (CDS) rose.

“The market reaction to the Nvidia news was swift. Nvidia fell 5% and closed the session below the $200-per-share mark. More importantly, Nvidia’s five-year CDS spiked, suggesting that it may not yet be the right time to buy the dip,” said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, a senior analyst at Swissquote.

title: Joe Biden interviews with memoir ghostwriter reveal him discussing sensitive information
description: Newly released audio tapes, disclosed by a conservative activist group, appear to show Joe Biden sharing classified information with a biographer and sometimes claiming memory lapses during interviews...
fullText:
Newly released audio tapes, disclosed by a conservative activist group, appear to show Joe Biden sharing classified information with a biographer and sometimes claiming memory lapses during interviews that occurred before his election to the presidency in 2020.

About three hours of audio and 117 pages of transcripts — with many redactions — were released by the Oversight Project, an arm of the Heritage Foundation, after Biden lost a prolonged legal fight to keep his conservations with his memoir ghostwriter, Mark Lewis Zwonitzer, private.

"They didn't even know I had this," Biden told Zwonitzer in October 2016, near the end of his second term as Barack Obama's vice president, as he talked about sensitive foreign policy matters handled by the administration.

In one 2017 session, after Biden had left the West Wing and before he'd launched his own presidential campaign, he appeared to admit retaining classified information from his time as vice president.

"I just found all the classified stuff downstairs," Biden said. "I wrote the President a handwritten 40-page memorandum arguing against deploying additional troops to Iraq -- I mean, to Afghanistan on the grounds that it wouldn't matter, that the day we left would be like the day before we arrived."

The potentially classified information itself is redacted in both the audio and transcripts that the Oversight Project released.

The right-wing group first sued to obtain the tapes after Special Counsel Robert Hur decided in 2024 not to charge Biden for how he handled classified information. Biden cooperated with Hur's inquiry and told the special prosecutor during his presidency that he did not intentionally mishandle any classified material.

Hur, who obtained the tapes as part of his inquiry, said in announcing his decision that he believed a jury would find Biden a sympathetic figure because of his age and what Hur described as a "poor memory" — a statement that became a flashpoint in public debate about Biden's age and fitness for the presidency.

Biden was 74 when the interviews began. He was 81 and seeking reelection when Hur released his report in early 2024, though Biden later ended his campaign for a second term after a halting debate performance against Republican Donald Trump.

The tapes contain instances of Biden being unable to recall some dates and details of topics he was discussing with Zwonitzer. Biden also showed a command of many details, recalling meetings and details of conversations referenced in the notes he shared.

At the Oversight Project, Vice President of Litigation Jeff Clark insisted the tapes prove Biden's decline.

"The tapes have always belonged to the American People, the Oversight Project just delivered them to their rightful owner," Clark said in a statement. "The knowledge of his deterioration was well-established."

A Biden spokesman blasted the release as politically motivated.

"President Biden's conversations for a book a decade ago that discussed his late son are private, and were provided to the Department of Justice on the express condition they stay that way," said TJ Ducklo. "Reversing course and making them public is just the latest example of this Administration weaponizing the DOJ for political retribution."

Biden initially sued to stop the Department of Justice from releasing the material, claiming the conversations were private. But he dropped his suit after a divided panel of appeals court judges rejected his bid. Biden could have petitioned the Supreme Court to intervene or asked for a rehearing by the full U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit.

In a 2-1 ruling, a three-judge panel from the circuit court found a "substantial" public interest in disclosing the material.

title: Trump orders signage claiming 'ideological capture' of Smithsonian
description: The new order comes after a scathing White House report, criticizing the museum.
fullText:
President Donald Trump ramped up his attacks against the Smithsonian Institution over the weekend by issuing an executive action that ordered new "temporary exhibits or signage" to be installed outside the National Museum of American History (NMAH), "warning" visitors about "the Ideological Capture" of the museum.

The "ideological capture" is a reference to allegations that the White House made against leaders at NMAH in a blistering July 4 report released by the White House Domestic Policy Council, accusing the museum and its leaders of presenting "a radical view of American history."

The report includes dozens of examples of exhibits and materials in exhibits that the White House has determined to be examples of "radical activism."

"Such signage shall notify visitors that the Museum exhibits should be renovated consistent with the findings in the Report and direct visitors to locations and resources for accurate information regarding America's history," Trump's executive order states.

Asked about the executive order, a spokesperson for the Smithsonian told ABC News on Monday they have "no comment at this time."

'The museum does not take sides': Smithsonian official defends institution amid Trump criticism

Trump ordered the Department of the Interior, which oversees the National Park Service, to install temporary signs "along the NPS-maintained sidewalks and walkways used by the public to access the Museum" to inform visitors of the findings of the White House report.

He also ordered the Interior Department to install new signage or exhibits on NPS-maintained land around the museum "that corrects inaccurate information presented in the Museum" regarding the 56 signers of the Declaration of Independence, claiming that the museum "failed to appropriately appropriately honor" on the nation's 250th anniversary in July.

ABC News reached out to the Interior Department and NPS to inquire about the timeline for installing new materials, but a request for comment was not returned.

NMAH Director Anthea Hartig pushed back against the White House's report while publicly testifying in a pair of House congressional hearings last week, where she asserted that the museum "does not take sides in America's political debates.

"Our work is governed by the Smithsonian standards of scholarship, accuracy, independence, and nonpartisanship," Hartig said in her opening remarks on Tuesday before a House Subcommittee on Delivering Government Efficiency. "The museum does not take sides in America's political debates. We preserve and document the evidence of American life in all of its breadth, so that the public can encounter the past and draw their own conclusions."

Hartig, who is the first top Smithsonian official to publicly address these accusations before Congress, added that while the Smithsonian "takes the concerns raised" in the White House report "seriously," the report "does not fairly or accurately" represent the museum's work.

"The Smithsonian takes the concerns raised in the White House Domestic Policy Council's report seriously, and as we continue to fact-check the report, we unwaveringly attest that it does not fairly or accurately characterize the full body of work at the museum," she said. "There is always room for improvement, but I also know the beauty and the inspiration and the expertise that lies in our collections, our exhibits, and our programming."

In scathing report, White House accuses Smithsonian of presenting 'a radical view of American history'

Hartig echoed comments made by Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch in an internal letter to staff that was obtained by ABC News.

"While there will always be room for improvement, this report is not a fair characterization of the work and totality of the National Museum of American History," Bunch, who has not addressed the report publicly, said in the letter. "At the Smithsonian, our work is driven by scholarship, accuracy, and an uncompromising commitment to tell the fullness of America's story."

The White House report was born out a review that was launched in response to Trump's March 27, 2025 executive order, "Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History."

The executive order directed Vice President J.D. Vance, in consultation with the president's advisers on domestic policy, "to remove improper ideology" from Smithsonian institutions, arguing that materials that cast America in a "negative light" have no place in federal cultural institutions.

"The serious concerns raised in this report are not about a few exhibits or a few controversial labels," the report says. "As it stands today, it would benefit most Americans, especially parents bringing their children for a tour, if the Smithsonian's flagship history museum had a label at every entrance that reads: 'Warning: the exhibits in this museum were prepared by people who don't want you to love your country.'"

Hartig pushed back against this claim on Tuesday and invited lawmakers to visit the museum to view its contents themselves.

"I believe what you will find, madams and sirs, is not an institution that has forgotten its country, but one that loves it enough to tell the full sweep of history, our triumphs and our struggles," she said. "I love the United States of America. I consider it the privilege of my career to help preserve its treasures and serve the American people."

Smithsonian chief disputes scathing White House report accusing museum of 'radical' activism

The Smithsonian Institution, which oversees 21 museums and galleries and the National Zoo, was established by Congress in 1846 and is both publicly and privately funded.

According to the Smithsonian Institution, it currently receives more than $1 billion in federal funding -- about 62% of its funding -- and the remainder of the funds come from "trust funds or non-federal funds, including contributions from private sources" and revenues from Smithsonian enterprises.

Bunch has been leading the Smithsonian since 2019 but the institution is overseen by a 17-member governing body, known as the Board of Regents. Bunch, who met with Trump at the White House on Aug. 28, 2025, repeatedly affirmed the Smithsonian's "independence" from political influence.

Referencing his conversations with Trump in a Sept. 3, 2025 letter to the institution's employees, Bunch underscored the independence of the Smithsonian, saying it was "paramount." He also told employees that the institution remains committed to telling the "American story" and "will always be, a place that welcomes all Americans and the world."

title: Explainer-France has seen its first 'fire-cloud'. What is it?
description: France is grappling with an unprecedented fire season that has led to the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of people and dealt a blow to the economy during
fullText:
July 28 (Reuters) - France is grappling with an unprecedented fire season that has led to the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of people and ‌dealt a blow to the economy during the peak tourist season.

But it's not ‌just the scale of the fires that is breaking new ground. They are also behaving in ways not seen ​before in France, including the formation of the country's first-ever reported pyrocumulonimbus, or "fire-cloud".

Below is a look at this rare phenomenon:

A pyrocumulonimbus is a cloud that forms above a large wildfire when intense heat drives smoke, ash and water vapour high into the atmosphere.

"You can ‌think of it as like a ⁠chimney, which is a fire at the bottom and the smoke going straight up a chimney into the stratosphere," David Bowman, professor of ⁠pyrogeography and fire science at the University of Tasmania, told Reuters.

While meteorologists can identify conditions that favour their formation, they cannot predict with precision when or where a fire-cloud will develop, said ​Jean-Christophe ​Vincendon, wildfire coordinator for the French national meteorological ​service.

Fire-clouds can ‌make wildfires more dangerous and less predictable by generating powerful winds that alter a fire's direction or producing lightning that ignites new blazes.

When they run out of energy, they can also trigger what's known as a "plume collapse".

"When the plume collapses, it's a showering of debris, burning debris," said Bowman.

WHAT DOES THIS MEAN FOR EUROPE?

French authorities said on Saturday that a ‌pyrocumulonimbus had been observed near Bordeaux, the first recorded ​in France.

The phenomenon presents an added challenge for ​emergency services because the erratic nature of ​fire outbreaks can force authorities to widen evacuation zones as a ‌precaution, said Marc Vermeulen, head of the ​Gironde fire and rescue ​service.

Bowman said Western Europe could now expect to see more of this phenomenon, which tends to occur in more extensive wilderness areas, such as in Canada or ​Australia.

"This is a very gravely ‌serious milestone," Bowman said. "It is fascinating, but it is also absolutely disastrous and ​terrible, and we just don't want more of these things."

title: Mitch McConnell's office releases new photo of senator amid health questions
description: The 84-year-old lawmaker was first hospitalized on June 14 after a fall and subsequently treated for pneumonia.
fullText:
WASHINGTON – Six weeks after he was hospitalized for a fall and pneumonia, Sen. Mitch McConnell's doctors still have not medically cleared him to return to work or leave a rehabilitation facility, the Capitol physician's office said.

Since June, the Kentucky Republican's health has been a source of widespread speculation and interest. He has missed 38 roll call votes in the Senate, including on key measures such as the annual defense policy bill and ending the Iran war, as well as high-profile confirmation hearings for crucial Trump nominees like Todd Blanche, who is awaiting a vote to become the next attorney general.

All summer his office has provided only limited updates on his condition. But in a statement July 27, McConnell, 84, said he was still having "intense physical therapy" and wouldn't be able to travel to western Kentucky for the annual Fancy Farm picnic, a marquee political event in the state.

"As always, I appreciate all of your continued well wishes, and I'm looking forward to getting back to the Senate and to Kentucky soon," he said.

The Office of the Attending Physician, which provides medical services and guidance to members of Congress, said the lifelong effects of McConnell's bout with childhood polio continue to be a "significant factor in his mobility." Doctors visit with him every day.

"Since his discharge from hospital care, he has maintained a strenuous course of physical therapy and rehabilitation, including multiple sessions a day designed to rebuild strength and reduce the risk of future falls," the office said in a statement.

McConnell also released a new photo, dated July 26, of himself alongside his wife, Elaine Chao. Though his Senate colleagues say they've talked to him several times by phone over the course of his absence, the former majority leader hasn't spoken publicly since his departure. He also hasn't given any external interviews.

His office did not provide a tentative date for when he could be expected back at work in the Senate, which is scheduled to depart for a monthlong recess in two weeks on Aug. 7.

Zachary Schermele is the congressional correspondent for USA TODAY. You can reach him by email at zschermele@usatoday.com. Follow him on X at @ZachSchermele and Bluesky at @zachschermele.bsky.social.

title: Is Lionel Messi playing MLS All-Star game? Inter Miami forward's status for 2026 Charlotte match vs. Liga MX XI
description: Lionel Messi is unquestionably the biggest draw of any player in Major League Soccer. His presence at the MLS All-Star game every year is a hot-button topic as fans hope to catch a glimpse of the Argentine at the showcase event.
fullText:
Is Lionel Messi playing MLS All-Star game? Inter Miami forward's status for 2026 Charlotte match vs. Liga MX XI originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Lionel Messi is unquestionably the biggest draw of any player in Major League Soccer.

Therefore, his presence at the MLS All-Star game every year is a hot-button topic as fans hope to catch a glimpse of the Argentine at the showcase event.

29 players were chosen to represent the league in the July 29 showcase match against an all-star roster from Liga MX in Mexico.

The Sporting News discusses whether Messi will be present for the match, and explains his whereabouts on the day.

MORE:How long will Lionel Messi be out for Inter Miami?

Lionel Messi will NOT be playing at the 2026 MLS All-Star game.

Having reached the 2026 FIFA World Cup final with Argentina, Messi has now earned rest and recovery time, as mandated by FIFA and the FIFPRO player's union.

Messi is allowed at least 21 days of rest from the day his team was eliminated before he can be mandated to return to action. The same is true for his club and international teammate Rodrigo De Paul, who will also miss the All-Star game for the same reason.

MORE: Players with the most goals in the history of the World Cup

No, Messi will not be suspended for his absence from the 2026 All-Star game.

The Argentina star was banned for one game last season after his unexcused absence for the 2025 All-Star match.

However, this time the absence is excused. FIFA and FIFPRO came to an agreement that all players must be given at least 21 days of rest at the end of each season. Even though the current MLS season is ongoing, FIFA considers the World Cup the "end of the season" as it relates to most European leagues, and therefore all World Cup players are allowed to enjoy this post-tournament rest before continuing activities.

MORE: The ultimate Messi-vs.-Ronaldo GOAT scorecard

Following the 21-day mandate from FIFA and FIFPRO, Lionel Messi and Rodrigo De Paul do not have to be back in training until at least August 9, or later if Inter Miami allow.

It is up to the club and the players to come to a mutual understanding on their return to play, and it's possible that Messi could ask for longer than the minimum allowed time given he is now 38 years old and his body may not recover as fast as most athletes closer to their prime.

It's also possible that Messi and De Paul return before the 21-day window closes, but only if they agree, as the club cannot mandate that action.

The initial starting XI for the MLS All-Star game is decided by a voting process that combines fan, player, and media selections.

From there, the rest of the roster is filled out by a selection of individuals chosen in tandem by the designated All-Star coaching staff (led in 2026 by Charlotte FC's Dean Smith, as Charlotte is the host city) and the league office.

Finally, the MLS commissioner is allowed to make final selections, as Don Garber elected to add two players to the squad for the 2026 game.

The following players were initially selected to the 2026 MLS All-Star roster but have withdrawn for an excused absence: Hugo Cuypers (Chicago Fire — transfer), Rodrigo De Paul (Inter Miami — rest), Mbekezeli Mbokazi (Chicago Fire — injury) and Lionel Messi (Inter Miami — rest)

title: Barcelona place €40 million price tag on 22-year-old homegrown midfielder – report
description: Barcelona have been keen on securing some sales since the start of the summer transfer window, with players like Ansu Fati and Inaki Pena leaving the club permanently.One other player the club have be...
fullText:
Barcelona have been keen on securing some sales since the start of the summer transfer window, with players like Ansu Fati and Inaki Pena leaving the club permanently.

One other player the club have been looking to sell since the start of the window is Marc Casado, with the 22-year-old losing prominence under Hansi Flick.

Now, according to Mundo Deportivo, Barcelona have set an asking price of €40 million for Marc Casado as the club remain open to selling the midfielder before the summer transfer window closes.

Flick has informed the club that they should listen to offers for the 22-year-old, believing Barcelona have enough depth in defensive midfield even after Frenkie de Jong’s injury.

The report claims Barcelona have already turned down one proposal that fell short of their valuation.

Barcelona open to Casado exit. (Photo by David Ramos/Getty Images)

With transfer fees continuing to rise across Europe and the Middle East this summer, the club believe €40 million is a fair price for Casado.

As a La Masia graduate, any transfer fee would count almost entirely as profit from a Financial Fair Play perspective, making a sale particularly attractive financially.

Casado is understood to be aware of the situation through his agent, Jorge Mendes, who has been discussing the player’s future with the club.

Interest from Saudi Arabia has not disappeared.

Barcelona are said to be monitoring the market closely after seeing clubs in the Saudi Pro League continue to spend heavily, and Casado could end up moving there.

The Spaniard’s role changed significantly last season.

Barça want €40 million for Casado. (Photo by Juan Manuel Serrano Arce/Getty Images)

After enjoying a breakthrough campaign in the 2024-25 season and earning his first Spain call-up, his playing time dropped considerably, making his long-term role under Flick less certain.

Selling Casado would not be an easy decision.

The midfielder represents exactly the type of academy graduate Barcelona have traditionally built around. He understands the club’s style, works tirelessly and still has room to develop at just 22 years old.

At the same time, Barcelona always have tremendous talent coming through midfield, and keeping a 22-year-old without giving him game time is not fair on the player.

If an offer close to €40 million arrives for a player Flick does not see as an undisputed starter, the club will face a serious decision.

For now, Casado remains part of the squad and has travelled with the team to England. It remains to be seen whether he is wearing Blaugrana next season.

The Eagles are reportedly about to send a bid to Brest for the 19-year-old centre-back. His former manager Eric Roy said, ‘He has great potential to work with.’

The Crystal Palace target made only six Ligue 1 appearances but still did enough to convince the South London club’s hierarchy of his potential and quality.

Palace will try to sign him as a replacement for Maxence Lacroix, who is on his way out of Selhurst Park for big money after two impressive seasons.

In his limited appearances, Le Guen won 80 percent of his aerial and 54% of his ground duels.

It remains unclear whether the addition of Le Guen will affect the pursuit of Chrislain Matsima, another target.

In reality, it shouldn’t. Palace lost Marc Guehi in January and never replaced him. Matsima should come in to fill that void.

After sorting their defence, the midfield is another area that demands immediate attention.

Cheick Doucoure has spent an extended period on the sidelines with injury, leaving the team without one of their most reliable ball-winners for much of the past 18 months.

Daichi Kamada’s departure has further reduced the club’s options, while uncertainty continues to surround Adam Wharton.

The England international is on the radar of several elite clubs, and they could pull the trigger before the window closes.

Even if Wharton stays, Palace are short on numbers and experience in the middle of the park.

Pierre Sage’s high-energy, transition-based system depends on athletic, technically secure midfielders capable of covering ground and controlling possession.

At present, the squad lacks the depth needed to cope with multiple competitions.

With the transfer window entering a crucial phase, Palace can no longer afford to wait. Reinforcements in midfield should be next on the agenda.

title: 'Classic manipulative behaviour' or 'the last step' for Arsenal?
description: Like everyone else, I am transfixed by the transfers happening every day in the Premier League.  It helps to have a lot of money and a brand name that attracts the top players.  Manchester City come to mind right away.
fullText:
Like everyone else, I am transfixed by the transfers happening every day in the Premier League. There is always the temptation to make a snap judgement of what has happened in the market so far, but this is unfair.

There is so much business still to be done and so many difficulties to overcome. Clubs often have to be sure that money is coming in from sales before they can spend on new players.

The gold standard is those who know what they want and move early because they have had a plan in place all along. It helps to have a lot of money and a brand name that attracts the top players.

Manchester City come to mind right away. With Rodri injured and Bernardo Silva gone, the move for Elliot Anderson, even at £116m, seems obvious and sensible in hindsight. Even without Pep Guardiola they are still title favourites alongside Arsenal because of that methodology.

But the Gunners have moved sensibly over the summer so far. Piero Hincapie was a no-brainer, particularly as William Saliba is injured, but I'd expect one more cover player in that position. What I didn't expect was a story suggesting that Vinicius Junior might be tempted to north London.

I hate being 'played' in these circumstances. Is Vini Jr, his agent or indeed Real Madrid just using Arsenal as a bargaining chip in contract talks?

This would be classic manipulative behaviour but if the chips are cashed in, it'd be an incredible win for Mikel Arteta. The Brazilian's wages feel wrong for Arsenal, but his addition would make that last step to becoming European champions far more likely.

You have to feel a little sorry for Christos Tzolis, just signed from Club Brugge for £34m, who might find that left flank suddenly a little crowded.

If Arsenal's use of physicality at corners is curtailed with changes to the rules, they'll need to find goals from another avenue. Maybe that is why Arteta feels the need to add more to an already impressive frontline.

title: Champions Saints host Newcastle on opening weekend
description: Prem champions Northampton host Newcastle on the opening weekend of the 2026-27 season, with Exeter at home to Gloucester.
fullText:
Champions Northampton will host Newcastle Red Bulls on the opening day of the 2026-27 Prem rugby season.

Saints beat Exeter to lift the trophy for the second time in three seasons in June and start the new campaign at home on Friday, 25 September.

The Chiefs are also at home for their first game, with Gloucester set to visit Sandy Park on the Saturday.

Elsewhere across opening weekend, Harlequins are at home to Bath on Friday, Sale host Bristol on Saturday evening and Leicester play Saracens in the only match on Sunday.

The 2026-27 Prem final will be held on Saturday, 19 June 2027 at the Allianz Stadium, Twickenham, with the season to take a series of breaks around international fixtures.

After five rounds in six weeks through September and October, there will be a four-week Prem break through November for the autumn matches of the Nations Championship.

With European competition beginning in December there are four Prem rounds across six weeks until January, before a 10-week league pause again in February and March for the Six Nations.

The new season also begins with promotion and relegation officially scrapped from the division.

While no club has been relegated from the Prem or promoted up from the Champ since Saracens in 2020 and 2021, this has now been formalised as part of a series of changes to English rugby voted through in February, as the league moves towards a franchise-style model.

Prem Rugby Cup pool fixtures announced

Prem relegation scrapped from 2026-27 season

A handful of matches next season will also be staged at major stadiums, as has become customary for some Prem clubs in recent years.

Harlequins play their two annual 'Big Game' fixtures at the Allianz Stadium, starting against Northampton, with the Prem's first-ever Monday night fixture on 28 December over the festive period.

They return to England's home stadium to play Newcastle in round 15 in May.

Gloucester are hoping to return to Villa Park after playing an inaugural game in Birmingham last season, however the venue is still to be finalised.

If all goes ahead they will again play Leicester in round 12 for the Slater Cup on the weekend of 27 March, while Bristol host the Cherry and Whites at Cardiff's Principality Stadium in a west country derby in round 13 three weeks later.

"There's huge momentum behind the Gallagher Prem heading into the new season, following a third consecutive sold-out final, significant international investment in our clubs, record broadcast audiences and soaring interest from younger fans," said Simon Massie-Taylor, chief executive officer of Prem Rugby.

"And following a landmark agreement to change our operating model earlier this year, we are well on the way with our plans to expand the league by the 2029/30 season," he added.

Northampton v Newcastle (19:45 BST)

Exeter v Gloucester (15:05 BST)

Leicester v Saracens (15:00 BST)

title: Lakers Proposed to Trade for 2 Ex-Luka Doncic Teammates in Mega Deal
description: This Lakers trade idea would reunite Luka Doncic with two of his former Mavericks teammates, P.J. Washington and Daniel Gafford. The post Lakers Proposed to Trade for 2 Ex-Luka Doncic Teammates in Mega Deal appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
The Los Angeles Lakers acquired nine new players this offseason, but they aren’t done making moves, with reports suggesting that they continue to pursue help at the five spot and the wing position. One Lakers trade idea would reunite Luka Doncic with two of his former Dallas Mavericks teammates, filling those needs.

Per multiple reports, the Dallas Mavericks are open to moving both Daniel Gafford and P.J. Washington as they prepare to usher in the Cooper Flagg era. Both role players played a key role in helping the Mavericks reach the 2024 NBA Finals and would be perfect additions due to their built-in chemistry with Doncic.

Lakers would receive: PJ Washington, Daniel Gafford

Mavericks would receive: Jarred Vanderbilt, Jaden Hardy, Jake LaRavia, Dalton Knecht, 2032 first-round pick swap (via LAL), 2031 second-round pick (via WAS), 2032 second-round pick (via WAS) and 2033 second-round pick (via LAL)

As Dallas users in the Cooper Flagg era, it makes little sense for the franchise to hold onto veterans like Daniel Gafford, P.J. Washington, Klay Thompson, Naji Marshall and possibly even Kyrie Irving. Several insiders expect them to gradually move all their veterans either this summer or by next year’s trade deadline, giving Flagg a roster of players that suit his timeline.

Furthermore, the Mavericks gave Gafford (three-year, $54M) and Washington (four-year, $88M) long-term extensions last year under the premise that Anthony Davis, Kyrie Irving, Klay Thompson and Co. would be there to lead a veteran outfit. However, their strategies have changed, and they appear to be heading in a youth movement.

The Mavs also need to reduce their logjam at the five spot, making Gafford dispensable. Their current rotation boasts of Dereck Lively II, new Santi Aldama, rookie Morez Johnson Jr. and Moussa Cissé, whom they are said to be very high on.

Adding the long-term money of Washington and Gafford comes with its fair share of risks, but could be one of the moves the Lakers need to make to give Luka Doncic a complete squad. Despite all their offseason acquisitions — including Walker Kessler, Quentin Grimes, Kevon Looney, Sandro Mamukelashvili, Collin Sexton, Ziaire Williams and Matisse Thybulle — the Lakers don’t really have a starting-caliber small forward, a role that P.J. Washington can slide into. While Grimes, Mamukelashvili and Sexton are offensively-skewed players, Williams and Thybulle are limited offensively. Washington would bring a more complete skill set with his three-point shooting and elite defense.

Similarly, the Lakers remain a little thin at the five spot despite adding Walker Kessler and Kevon Looney. While the latter is more of an energy guy who plays limited minutes, Kessler is coming off a season-ending injury and may need some insurance.

A player like Gafford would be perfect as a second-string big for the Lakers, who continue to pursue the market for a big man, according to The Athletic’s Dan Woike.

“The Lakers are still monitoring the market for big men, team sources told The Athletic,” Woike reported last week. “They traded for Walker Kessler and signed Kevon Looney to play center, and Mamukelashvili can play the position, too.

“The team could address the position either by trade or signing, like with potentially adding Thybulle. The roster is currently at full capacity.”

title: Real Madrid icon Nacho backs Mourinho for success at the Bernabeu: ‘Great things are coming’
description: Speaking to AS in an interview, former Real Madrid captain and club legend Nacho Fernandez has backed new manager Jose Mourinho to lead the team back to the top after two underwhelming seasons.Los Bla...
fullText:
Speaking to AS in an interview, former Real Madrid captain and club legend Nacho Fernandez has backed new manager Jose Mourinho to lead the team back to the top after two underwhelming seasons.

Los Blancos have brought Mourinho back this summer after last season’s debacle when the team failed to win any trophy and struggled to perform at the expected level under both Xabi Alonso and Alvaro Arbeloa.

Given the situation, where there has been a lot of tension in the dressing room and the lack of trophies, Nacho believes that Mourinho is the right man to lead Real Madrid back to the top.

The former Spanish international highlighted how the manager holds a special place in his career, having handed him his first-team debut with Los Blancos.

“Well, for me and my whole family, Mourinho is a special person. He’s the coach who has shaped my career, the one who gave me my debut, the one who gave me the opportunity…,” he said.

“I made my debut that day, but I’d already done preseason training with him. After that match at Mestalla, many more games with the first team followed. Mou will always be special to me.”

Mourinho is back at Madrid. (Photo courtesy: Real Madrid official website)

Continuing, he added: “Regardless of the fact that he’s a great coach, which he is, for me and my whole family, he’s the coach, so to speak. What can I say? I wish him all the best in this second spell.

“I think a coach is coming in who’s exactly what Real Madrid needs right now, a bit of a challenge. I remember that period as one of the best of my life.

“I was also at a time when we were doing very well at Castilla. That’s where it all started for me at Real Madrid. And I’m very happy and very grateful, of course, to Mou.”

Talking about the changes that Real Madrid can expect to see with Mourinho in charge, Nacho explained:

“What I am sure of is that I don’t know if they’ll ultimately win titles, because this is football and it’s not easy, but he will definitely have the players fully committed, giving 100%.

“The intensity he brings to every training session and every match, having been on the inside, I can assure you it’s 100%. So, if the players and Mourinho can all pull together, I have no doubt that good things are coming for Real Madrid.

“Mou is a Real Madrid fan, he’s a Madridista. That’s what’s important; he knows perfectly well what it means to win and what it means to lose at this club. If the players are fully behind him, great things are coming for Real Madrid…”

In recent years, Real Madrid have had to bid goodbye to several club icons like Toni Kroos, Lucas Vazquez, Luka Modric, and Nacho himself, something that the Spaniard believes has hurt the team.

Nacho left Real Madrid in 2024. (Photo by Angel Martinez/Getty Images)

Dani Carvajal has also joined the list, having left the club this summer after his contract expired.

“Absolutely. I think without a doubt, and not just at Real Madrid. I believe that ultimately, at any club, it’s important to have homegrown talent, especially Spanish players, who have experienced what Real Madrid is all about since they were children,” he said.

“They teach you how to win, how to respect your opponent, how to always give your all, how to fight until the last minute. I think these things are fundamental, especially at a club with the demands of Real Madrid.

“And if you also manage to have foreign players, like you said, Modric or Kroos, who seem like academy graduates because after so many years they’ve become so ingrained in the club’s philosophy, it’s a consequence of all the titles we’ve won.”

On whether he will return to Real Madrid in the future in any capacity, Nacho replied: “Real Madrid is my home, that’s for sure. I can’t tell you exactly how, but whatever they need, I’ll be there without a doubt.

“I haven’t even thought about what I’m going to do, or how, or what I’m going to do after football. Madrid is my home, and I’ll be there for them whenever they need me.”

title: MLS make Lionel Messi exception over punishment rule that left him ‘very upset’ in 2025
description: The MLS have decided to exempt Lionel Messi from the huge punishment that they imposed on him in 2025. With the FIFA World Cup ending just a little over a week ago, many have wondered when Lionel Messi would return to Inter Miami.
fullText:
The MLS have decided to exempt Lionel Messi from the huge punishment that they imposed on him in 2025.

With the FIFA World Cup ending just a little over a week ago, many have wondered when Lionel Messi would return to Inter Miami.

Messi helped lead Argentina to the FIFA World Cup final and has been away from his club side since then as he recovers, which will force him to miss one of the MLS’s landmark events.

Lionel Messi is confirmed to be missing the 2026 MLS All-Star week in Charlotte, North Carolina, as he takes time away from Inter Miami following a grueling FIFA World Cup.

MLS officials confirmed to ESPN that Messi will not receive a one-match suspension for missing the festivities, the standard punishment issued to players.

However, this isn’t a case of Messi receiving preferential treatment as a star player, as the MLS had agreed to let players participating in the FIFA World Cup get some time off to recover.

This is why Messi and Rodrigo de Paul are exempt from the punishment, as a statement from the MLS revealed:

“Prior to the start of the 2026 season, Major League Soccer and the MLS Players Association agreed that upon a player’s exit from the World Cup competition, clubs would have individual conversations with each player to determine the appropriate rest and return to training and competition timeline.

“Consistent with that agreement, Rodrigo De Paul and Lionel Messi will be excused from participating in the 2026 MLS All-Star Game.”

This decision is a stark contrast to last year, when Messi, along with Jordi Alba, received a one-match suspension for missing the event.

This decision was criticized by Miami Heat co-owner Jorge Mas last year, who revealed how upset Messi was over the ‘draconian’ punishment.

“Lionel Messi is very upset, like we all are in the club, with the fact that they won’t be able to play tomorrow night.

“But I think what we have to do as a club is to get together as one, have an attitude that is us against the world… I think that the punishment for the rule is frankly draconian.

“Obviously, it was not a positive reaction [from Messi and Alba]. They want to compete, they want to play games.

“That’s what they’re here for, to play and win. They understand the magnitude of tomorrow night’s game.

“So no, their reaction was exactly as expected of two competitive players who don’t understand the decision, who don’t understand why not attending an exhibition match leads directly to a suspension.”

description: Co-hosts Gaz Drinkwater and Joe McGrath discussed which players impressed them in Manchester United's comfortable pre-season win over Rosenborg in the latest episode of BBC Radio Manchester's The Devils' Advocate podcast. fullText:
Co-hosts Gaz Drinkwater and Joe McGrath discussed which players impressed them in Manchester United's comfortable pre-season win over Rosenborg in the latest episode of BBC Radio Manchester's The Devils' Advocate podcast.

Drinkwater was full of praise for Joshua Zirkzee, who scored a "Puskas award nominee" goal in the friendly, slaloming his way past defenders and goalkeeper before tapping into an empty net.

"It was a great goal and really nice to watch," he said.

"It did kind of look like United were playing on Fifa with the difficulty [level] set on amateur. It was so slow the way it happened and there's no way a goal like that would be scored in the Premier League, but I'm not saying that to discount Joshua Zirkzee or take anything away from him. It was a lovely goal."

On Zirkzee being linked with a move away from Old Trafford, Drinkwater added: "At times, he comes on and is the exact type of player you need in a game. I like a lot of his attributes and you can tell by the way he plays that he would do very well in the Italian league.

"He plays just a little bit slower but he is really, really good on the ball. He is so slick but he needs to play in a slower league.

"He's one of those players who is too good for the role we want him to play, which is very occasionally coming on and making an impact, and very rarely starting games. I wouldn't mind if we let him go."

title: Glenn McGrath calls Jasprit Bumrah 'spring chicken': Australia legend tells India pacer to increase longevity
description: Aussie legend Glenn McGrath called Jasprit Bumrah a 'spring chicken' and shared key workload advice for the Indian pacer to maximize his career longevity.
fullText:
Glenn McGrath calls Jasprit Bumrah 'spring chicken': Australia legend tells India pacer to increase longevity originally appeared on Cricket News. Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Glenn McGrath calls Jasprit Bumrah, 32, still young and urges format prioritisation.

Recent injuries hit India's pace unit, including Bumrah and Prince Yadav.

McGrath urges bowlers to build strength, not caution, against breakdowns.

Australian pace legend Glenn McGrath has weighed in on Jasprit Bumrah's ongoing fitness concerns and described the Indian spearhead as a 'spring chicken' who is still relatively young in cricketing terms. However, he suggested that Bumrah might need to figure out a way to stretch his career further, potentially by cutting back his workload in one of the three formats.

Ever since the international calendar resumed following the IPL back in June, India's fast bowling stocks have been repeatedly tested by injuries. Bumrah's own participation in the upcoming Test series against Sri Lanka remains uncertain, while fellow pacer Prince Yadav also picked up an injury during the recent Zimbabwe tour.

Mayank Yadav only recently returned to international duty after being sidelined for two years, and given India's packed year-round schedule, the team management has increasingly leaned on a rotation strategy to manage player workloads.

MORE: Laxman praises Sooryavanshi's maturity after heroics vs Zimbabwe

McGrath, who works with the MRF Pace Foundation, said the decision on how to manage Bumrah's career will ultimately rest with the bowler himself.

“Well again it’s up to him what he wants. How old’s Bumrah now? 31- 32? He’s only a spring chicken. So he’s got to find a way to have a bit of longevity," he said.

According to McGrath, much of the path forward depends on what Bumrah himself wants, whether that means prioritising Test cricket or shifting focus more toward the shorter formats, alongside how his body continues to respond over time.

"He’s had a few injuries unfortunately, but he’s class, a quality bowler. Just see what he wants to do," McGrath said.

"That’s what it comes down to: whether he wants to focus on Test cricket or whether he just wants to play T20. It also depends on his body. And like I said, guys who hyper-extend their arm do place a bit more stress through that joint there. So we’ll see what the future holds."

MORE: 'Abhishek sorted out': Srikkanth believes Samson will return to India T20I side

Beyond Bumrah specifically, McGrath used the opportunity to share broader thoughts on how fast bowlers are managed in the modern game, arguing that players should be conditioned to handle the physical demands of pace bowling rather than being overly shielded from potential breakdowns.

“It’s the nature of the beast being a fast bowler; it’s not a natural action so injuries are part of the game,” McGrath said.

"Where I’m a little disappointed these days, and it’s probably been that way a little bit for a long time, is that they put them (fast bowlers) in cotton wool. We try to nurse them back to full fitness, and we protect them."

MORE: Why is 33-year-old Saransh Jain included in India Test squad for SL tour

In his view, extended rehabilitation stints often do more harm than good, since months spent recovering can leave a player's overall fitness and strength trailing far behind where it needs to be.

"The best way to do it is to get stronger than the stresses of fast bowling. To do a rehab program for months and months puts your fitness and your strength so far behind that you’ve got so far to catch up."

After tearing his side muscle and dropping to just 77 kilograms, McGrath said he realised a change was necessary if he wanted a sustainable career, a turning point that led him to work closely with trainer Kevin Chevell, who helped make him considerably more durable over time.

"Getting physically stronger and fitter doesn’t mean bowling hours in the nets or working on the wrong things in the gym," McGrath opined.

"I got stronger than the stresses of fast bowling and very rarely got injured. So instead of putting him in cotton wool, we should be actually making him unbreakable, getting him working hard.

"When I tore my side muscle, I lost a heap of weight. I weighed 77 kilograms, so I realised if I keep doing what I’m doing, I’m not going to last very long. That’s why I went down the train and Kevin Chevell (training), who’s working here with the boys and he made me unbreakable."

MORE: 'How can I plan?': Samson on his India future at 2028 T20 WC amid Sooryavanshi's rise

McGrath's stance carries weight given his own remarkable longevity, but applying his era's approach directly to today's game overlooks how drastically fast bowlers' schedules have changed.

Modern quicks like Bumrah juggle franchise cricket, bilateral series and global tournaments almost year-round, a workload McGrath never had to manage across three formats simultaneously. Building physical resilience is undeniably important, but so is smart load management in a calendar this congested, something India's rotation policy already attempts to address rather than pure over-caution.

Bumrah's hyper-extension action also isn't comparable to a standard side strain, it's a structural factor that genuinely increases injury risk regardless of conditioning levels. McGrath's broader point about strength training holds value, but reducing Bumrah's fitness challenges purely to a mindset issue risks oversimplifying a much more complex modern problem.

Should Bournemouth decide that a sale is the most practical outcome, interest from multiple clubs could accelerate negotiations. Both Arsenal and Chelsea appear to be monitoring developments closely as they weigh up their next steps.

title: Why the Tigers should (and shouldn't) trade star ace Tarik Skubal at the 2026 MLB trade deadline
description: The Tigers have a decision to make on Tarik Skubal. Here's what they will have to consider.
fullText:
Why the Tigers should (and shouldn't) trade star ace Tarik Skubal at the 2026 MLB trade deadline originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Every contender is looking for an upgrade ahead of the MLB trade deadline, but no player might be more coveted than Tigers ace Tarik Skubal.

The two-time Cy Young Award winner is a pending free agent and has been viewed as a trade candidate since the Tigers fell as many as 16 games under .500 early in the season.

With better results in recent weeks, however, Detroit could still hold on to Skubal and try to make another run at the postseason.

What's the right decision? Here are the cases for and against the Tigers trading Skubal.

MORE:16 players who could be traded by MLB deadline

Barring a drastic change of heart, the Tigers aren't going to re-sign Skubal. The two sides have reportedly remained far apart in contract talks, and the record-setting $13 million gap between Skubal and the Tigers during the arbitration process was likely the final nail in the coffin.

With that in mind, if the Tigers held on to Skubal for the remainder of the season, what would it take to make that decision a success? If it's strictly a World Series win, you can probably take that idea off the table. Not only are the Tigers still comfortably under .500, but there isn't any reason to believe they have the talent to win a championship.

Is it a trip to the World Series? The American League is wide open, but if the Tigers couldn't get past the ALDS last season, that's hard to envision. If the ALCS, which is also unlikely, would justify keeping Skubal, Detroit should think long and hard about whether that's a worthwhile goal.

From a practical standpoint, making the postseason is unlikely. The Tigers are facing a six-game deficit in the AL Central, which is manageable, but they have three teams ahead of them rather than just one team to chase down. Detroit is closer in the wild-card race but faces the same dynamic, with four teams separating the franchise from the final wild-card team.

Skubal is coming off two excellent starts, his best since returning from the injured list. If he isn't coming back next season, it makes more sense to go get some value instead of holding on to a pipe dream of a magical October run.

MORE:Tarik Skubal makes trade deadline stance clear

The Tigers might not want their reputation to be that of a team that had a chance at the postseason and threw it away by dealing a beloved ace. With the American League so mediocre and the final wild-card team hovering near .500, Detroit could set a goal of 83-85 wins and enter a wild-card series with one of baseball's elite pitchers setting the tone in Game 1.

Looking around the AL, only two teams are more than six games over .500: the Rays, who still have to prove that they can win in October, and the Yankees, who have held their own in the second half but are struggling to find any offense with Aaron Judge, Giancarlo Stanton and now Cody Bellinger injured.

The Tigers may see 2026 as their year to make a run in October — if they can get there. Getting there with Skubal is challenging. Getting there without Skubal is just about impossible.

The value Detroit would have been able to get for Skubal earlier in his contract would have been immense, but the value for him as a rental might not be enough to totally transform the organization. If that's the case, the Tigers can show their fans that they aren't willing to quit on the season and give this group a real chance to make a push.

MORE: Every Cy Young winner in the history of the award

Skubal is set to be a free agent after this season. The Tigers ace is making $32 million after the salary arbitration process ruled in his favor over Detroit's significantly lower $19 million offer.

That gap has convinced most fans that Skubal is headed elsewhere in free agency in the winter, and Skubal recently made comments that alluded to some lingering tension between himself and the front office.

If the Tigers decide their best bet is to keep Skubal and try to engineer a miraculous postseason run, they run the risk of getting no talent back for one of the best pitchers in baseball, much like the Angels when they held onto Shohei Ohtani at the 2023 deadline.

title: Disney+ removes 4K and HDR from premium plans in Germany
description: Disney+ no longer streams 4K and HDR in Germany. Even premium customers only see 1080p in SDR. The cause is unclear.
fullText:
Since the weekend, Disney+ has not been streaming in 4K resolution or HDR in Germany. Even subscribers to the most expensive premium plan are only seeing films and series in a maximum of 1080p and SDR, as heise online was able to confirm on several editorial devices.

The labels for “4K Ultra HD” and “HDR” have disappeared across the board in the app and apparently across all device categories. Caschy's Blog first reported this. So far, there is no direct mention of the restriction on Disney+'s official help pages regarding video quality. 4K is still advertised there for the premium subscription, but HDR is not mentioned. Disney has not immediately confirmed a request from heise online.

A connection to the patent dispute that has been occupying Disney+ in Germany for months seems likely – but it is not yet proven. At the beginning of the year, Disney had initially removed Dolby Vision, HDR10+, and 3D content from its German offering, before the standard HDR10 format followed. Disney cited a “court proceeding before a German patent court” as the reason at the time.

Behind this is a legal dispute with the US company InterDigital. In November, the Munich Regional Court ruled that Disney+ infringes InterDigital's rights when streaming videos with dynamic HDR images and issued a preliminary injunction. Disney subsequently re-enabled HDR10, while Dolby Vision and HDR10+ remained unavailable in Germany.

On July 23, InterDigital was able to obtain a further injunction against Disney from the Düsseldorf local chamber of the Unified Patent Court (UPC), which concerns HEVC encoding. “HEVC encoding is a critical component of the high-quality, premium viewing experience that streaming companies like Disney use to justify higher subscription prices”, commented InterDigital's Chief Legal Officer on the decision in a press release.

Disney+'s premium subscription costs 16 euros per month or 160 euros per year. It differs from the standard subscription for 11 euros primarily through 4K, HDR, Dolby Atmos, and four parallel streams. Of these added values, only the audio and the number of streams currently remain.

Even when the HDR formats were removed, the Consumer Advice Centre of Lower Saxony advised subscribers to claim back a portion of the subscription price paid. The exact reason for the poorer quality is irrelevant to customers, a spokesperson for the consumer advice centre told dpa. “Legally, Disney+ as their contractual partner is solely responsible for ensuring the advertised and paid-for quality.” The consumer advocates do not provide a sample letter, so affected customers must contact Disney individually.

title: The Uses of 'Treason'
description: the press as traitors, Trump is trying to solidify his splintering MAGA base.
fullText:
On May 15, as Donald Trump and his entourage flew back to the United States from a state visit to China, the president ambled to the back of Air Force One for a gaggle with the traveling press corps. David E. Sanger—the New York Times’ White House and national security correspondent—stood face to face with Trump, his phone stretched up to just below the president’s mouth, appearing to record his words. Sanger asked about the war with Iran. “What would the use be of repeating the bombing? You did it for thirty-eight days, and you did not get the political changes in Iran—” Trump jumped in: “No, I got, I had a total military victory,” he said, touting his administration’s supposed successes. Then he leaped into a tirade against the press. “I actually think it’s sort of treasonous what you write,” Trump concluded. “And you should know better, David. You know better. Your editors tell you what to write, and you write it, and you should be ashamed of yourself. I actually think it’s treason.”

Over the past decade, Trump has repeatedly suggested that people he views as his adversaries—journalists, politicians in Congress and the White House, federal bureaucrats, and activists, to name a few—are traitors to the nation. Trump has always had a hard time distinguishing between the national interest and his own whims, so it’s perhaps no big shock that he routinely confuses dissent with treason. But these pronouncements have seemed increasingly common lately. Last fall, after a group of Democratic lawmakers posted a video reminding military servicepeople that they can refuse illegal orders, Trump accused them of “SEDITIOUS BEHAVIOR, punishable by DEATH!” (The administration’s attempt to bring a federal indictment against the lawmakers failed, and was eventually abandoned.) In March, the White House, in an official release, accused CNN of trying to “undermine our decisive victories” in the US-Israeli war on Iran, and Trump posted on Truth Social that some outlets “should be brought up on Charges for TREASON for the dissemination of false information!” Last month, he lashed out at the Times again—for an analysis that explored how the decision to wage the war had changed very little geopolitically—alleging “TREASONOUS” stories and warning: “I will be adding all of their false and ridiculous reporting to my multi Billion Dollar lawsuit against them. They are Criminals!” Trump has written or reshared social media posts featuring the word “treason” more than fifty times since 2016, according to Roll Call. These comments are often erroneous, legally incoherent, or delivered in clumsy asides during speeches, but they tend to be united by a sense of rage at anyone appearing to undermine Trump’s personal authority. “There is no more serious charge a commander in chief can make against an independent news organization,” A.G. Sulzberger, the publisher of the Times, wrote after Trump called the paper treasonous during his first term. As Margaret Sullivan put it in The Guardian recently, this is “the language and the strategy of authoritarian states.”

To point out the obvious, none of the things Trump has described as such come close to amounting to treason. To prevent abuse by a would-be despot, the framers of the Constitution sketched a very narrow definition of the term—which is the only crime explicitly defined in the document—as levying war against the United States, “or in adhering to their Enemies, giving them Aid and Comfort.” But that does not make Trump’s constant drumbeat of accusations something we should normalize or ignore. One of Trump’s goals, as some observers have noted, is to bully, threaten, and shame news organizations with enough ferocity that they soften their scrutiny. (In some cases this appears to have worked; CBS News and its parent company, Paramount Skydance, have sought to curry favor with the Trump administration.) The cries of treason are also part of Trump’s long-standing push to delegitimize the independent press. “You know why I do it?”—insult the press, that is—“I do it to discredit you all and demean you all so when you write negative stories about me, no one will believe you,” Trump reportedly said in 2016 to Lesley Stahl, the 60 Minutes correspondent, according to her telling. And then, of course, there is Trump’s tendency to bruise easily from bad publicity, stretching back to his days as a real estate developer and tabloid darling in the eighties.

Yet Trump’s claims of treason, to me, stem from a more sinister impulse—and represent more serious offenses—than his day-to-day abuse. Accusing an opponent of this highest of crimes, or smearing them as a traitor, is an attempt to enforce a particular vision of political belonging. By deploying these terms, a speaker carves a wound into the body politic, defining who is part of it on one side, and who is banished as disloyal on the other. By branding journalists as traitors, Trump is telling his base that the press—instead of being a load-bearing pillar of America’s ongoing experiment with democracy—is in fact a fifth column, an enemy within, a parasite that must be purged. In this way, Trump’s exclusionary rhetoric helps reveal the violence that has always been necessary to tie his political movement together. As the intertwined threads of the MAGA coalition loosen over Jeffrey Epstein, the war in Iran, the rising cost of living, and questions of succession, Trump’s language has become increasingly martial, as he tries to keep his base from unraveling.

On May 15, Sanger, following Trump’s rant at him on Air Force One, went on X and reshared a post from @NYTimesPR—written in the direct, rapid-response style that has become characteristic of that account in recent months—which quoted Charlie Stadtlander, a Times spokesperson. “Reporting isn’t treason. It’s foundational to a free press and the work that America’s founders wrote the First Amendment to protect,” Stadtlander had written. “We will continue this important, constitutionally protected work.”

Has America ever needed a media defender more than now? Help us by joining CJR today.
