title: NI's Olympic champions struggle on medal-less Monday
description: BBC Sport NI looks at Olympic champions Rhys McClenaghan and Daniel Wiffen's struggles as both missed out on Commonwealth medals on Monday.
fullText:
"Olympic champion is feeling rusty at the Commonwealth Games."

Those were the words of 800m freestyle Olympic gold medallist Daniel Wiffen, but they equally could have come from or been applied to his fellow Olympic champion Rhys McClenaghan on the pommel horse.

It was meant to be a magical Monday for Northern Ireland at the Commonwealth Games, with both Paris 2024 champions in action.

The expectation was that they could be the two, given their previous winning pedigree, to land NI's first two gold medals in Glasgow.

It was more mediocre than magic though as both struggled in their favourite events, so much so they did not even make it to the podium, with McClenaghan sixth in the pommel horse final and Wiffen fourth in the 800m decider.

McClenaghan was a master of his own downfall, starting slowly with his new routine and finishing in even worse fashion, but he was not too downcast by his performance and wanted to focus instead on how it was a step towards a bigger goal with the next Olympics two years away.

He said that while the routine obviously "didn't go to plan" it was "another stepping stone to what's to come" on his journey back to the ultimate pinnacle of retaining Olympic gold.

Wiffen is also building for two years' time, but he was much more self-critical, stating that he "didn't know what was going on" with his display as he was outclassed by the strong Australian trio of Sam Short, Benjamin Goedemans and Matthew Galea.

"They [the Australians] have come to play, and I haven't to be honest," Wiffen said.

"I thought I would at least be a 7:42 time coming into this [he swam 7:48.82] and honestly I just felt a bit rusty coming into this.

"I did try to push it, but I just felt my stroke was all over the place."

McClenaghan finishes sixth in pommel horse final

Wiffen finishes fourth in tough 800m final

Besides their struggles on Monday, it is easy to draw parallels between the two that stretch beyond their status as Olympic gold medallists.

They were both operating at the very peak of their powers at the end of the last Olympic cycle in 2024 which helped to yield golds for both in Paris.

Then injuries struck and hit hard last year.

McClenaghan opted to go for surgery on a troublesome shoulder problem that kept him out of action for the entirety of 2025.

The Commonwealth Games are his first major event since Paris almost two years ago.

Wiffen suffered from appendicitis in June 2025 which had lasting effects that led him to pull out of the Worlds in July last year.

While he won gold in the 1500m in the European Short Course Championships, he was third in the 800m at the same meet in Lubin.

Both are now in the position of having to use 2026 to rebuild, and a medal of any colour in their favourite events would no doubt have strengthened both their feelings of being on the way back to the very top.

McClenaghan had a simple solution to his issues: to go back to the gym to "progress even more" with the Europeans upcoming in August and the Worlds in October.

Wiffen may need to do some further self-examination to find the cure to his ails, with the "nerves" he spoke about post-race obviously not being used as fuel for good performances as he felt he was "not handling them well".

While McClenaghan will have to wait until next month to write the wrongs of his display in the Glasgow International Arena, Wiffen has a chance to bounce back quickly and in style with a medal in the 1500m final on Wednesday.

His previous silver in the Commonwealth Games came in that event four years ago and a repeat at Tollcross Swimming Centre later this week would be a major confidence boost before the Europeans in two weeks' time.

"I'm going to learn from this," Wiffen said. "Normally, when I have a bad couple of swims the 1500m brings a brighter side out of it, so we will see how it goes on Wednesday.

"I hope I can go into it with a positive mindset and see what happens. I'll hopefully come back with a medal, then I will be happy.

"The main goal is the gold in LA so we're working towards that."

title: Young and Hahn win England's first athletics golds
description: Sprinters Thomas Young and Sophie Hahn pick up gold medals for England on the opening night of athletics at the Commonwealth Games.
fullText:
Sprinters Thomas Young and Sophie Hahn picked up gold medals for England on the opening night of athletics at the Commonwealth Games.

Both won their races in the men's and women's 100m T38 finals in Glasgow with Young doing so to mark his 26th birthday in style.

Young, who missed out on the 2022 Games with an injury, recorded a season's best and Games record time of 11:11 seconds.

"It might be the best birthday I've ever had," he said. "It's actually joint with Fulham winning in the play-offs on my 20th, but it's probably this to be fair. Just. I've not had my birthday cake yet. I was eyeing up a chocolate cake in the hotel so if they're still open I'll have some of that."

In the women's final, Hahn beat Team Wales captain and defending champion Olivia Breen into second place, triumphing with a time of 12:79, with England team-mate Maddie Down posting a personal best of 12:86 to secure a bronze medal.

"This is very special," said Hahn. "It's been a long time since I last won a Commonwealth Games back in 2018. This means a lot to come here in a home Games and to win."

British champion Sam Bennett won silver in the men's 110m hurdles final with a personal best time of 13:30 as he was beaten by Jamaica's Demario Prince. England's Tade Ojoro missed out on a medal in fifth.

Kimani Jack, 22, secured a bronze in the men's high jump final with a jump of 2.20m, with the gold medal going to Jamaica's Romaine Beckford who cleared 2.25m.

"I really really loved it out there, it was a great experience," said Jack. "I've said it multiple times but shout out Glasgow, they know how to put on an event."

In round one of the women's 800m, Olympic silver medallist Georgia Hunter Bell won her heat in two minutes 02.61 seconds to finish ahead of Scotland's Jemmie Reekie as both qualified.

"I was happy to control it and I felt really good," said Hunter Bell. "I'm happy and it's job done.

"I've never done the Commonwealth Games before, so it's obviously my debut. For me, it was always going to be a no-brainer that I do it."

title: Diomande agrees Real Madrid terms as PSG step away
description: RB Leipzig winger Yan Diomande agrees personal terms with Real Madrid after Paris St-Germain withdraw their interest.
fullText:
RB Leipzig winger Yan Diomande has agreed personal terms with Real Madrid after Paris St-Germain withdrew their interest.

The 19-year-old Ivory Coast international was previously a target for Liverpool, who had an initial bid of £69m rejected in June, as well as PSG.

Liverpool then moved on to other targets, and PSG have now opted against entering a bidding war with Real.

PSG are said to have had a final £102.5m bid rejected for the teenager on Sunday.

Madrid have since agreed personal terms, said to be modelled on England midfielder Jude Bellingham's contract as they are incentivised on performances and effectively improve year-on-year.

Real will pay more than £100m for Diomande, who joined Leipzig from Spanish club Leganes last summer on a five-year deal.

'Everything I do is for you' - how tragedy is driving Diomande

Sources close to Real say key negotiators Jose Angel and Juni Calafat have been scouting Diomande for about five years, but were not reactive to Diomande's World Cup performances.

PSG had been frontrunners for the Ivorian until Real registered their interest, and they confirmed their withdrawal from the race on Sunday.

"The asking transfer fee and salary demands were completely disproportionate and distortive - and PSG will not break its principles of rational financial management and squad balance," the French club said.

"As a two-time consecutive Champions League winner and the most successful club in recent years, PSG will also not engage in the inflationary and manipulative games of certain player agents - and will instead calmly and confidently continue its transfer planning."

Leipzig have tried hard to keep the forward in Germany but regard the interest in Diomande as extraordinary, so have found it difficult to reject the interest - and potential record sale price - from Europe's elite clubs.

Diomande was the Bundesliga's young player of the season for 2025-26, having scored 12 goals and registered eight assists last term.

He moved from his native Ivory Coast to an academy in the United States in 2025 before joining Spanish side Leganes.

title: Glasgow roars for new Scottish heroes as Sandilands & Bryce claim glory
description: Day one of the athletics at the 2026 Commonwealth Games was set up perfectly to be the final act in Eilish McColgan's odyssey. Luckily for Glasgow, other heroes emerged.
fullText:
Day one of the athletics at the Commonwealth Games was set up perfectly to be the final act in Eilish McColgan's odyssey.

The script was written for the 2022 triumphant hero to complete her gruelling journey - from injury back to her homeland - to see off any challengers to her crown.

It was not meant to be. McColgan was forced to withdraw after failing to recover from a foot injury.

Luckily for the roaring Scotstoun crowd, other heroes in blue emerged.

Ben Sandilands and Steven Bryce took home gold and bronze respectively in the men's T20 1500m, roared on by the Scottish crowd.

Sandilands was rapid around the final lap, clocking a time of 3:57.20, while Bryce held on for third, just behind Canadian Michael Barber.

Scotland's Lynn surprises himself to join Ward on pommel podium

Evans steps out of shadows into spotlight with Scotland's fourth gold

Commonwealth Games medal table and results

Megan Keith was the sole Scottish representative in the women's 10,000m after McColgan dropped out.

Despite a swell of cheers from the crowd at every pass, the Inverness runner was unable to replicate the iconic 2022 performance of her compatriot, finishing ninth in a time of 32:22.11.

Canada's formidable Olympic hammer champion Ethan Katzberg drew gasps of awe from the Glasgow crowd with his herculean throw of 80.97m, which set a Commonwealth record.

But the biggest cheers in the hammer were reserved for Scotland's Chris Bennett, competing in his fourth and final Games.

He finished fifth with his longest throw of 69.48m, clearly emotional as he wrapped up a 24-year career.

Alexander Thomson - who trains just down the road at Victoria Park and had fought back from knee surgery - finished ninth in the T38 100m final.

Jemma Reekie comfortably booked her place in the semi-finals of the 800m, finishing second in her heat with a time of 2:03.09 behind England's world indoor 1,500m champion Georgia Hunter Bell.

Erin Wallace also booked her place in the semi-finals with a time of 2:03.15, but Mena Scatchard just missed out on qualification by 0.06 seconds after finishing fourth in her heat.

In the early sessions, Stephen Mackenzie got Scotland off to a strong start as he progressed to the men's long jump final on Wednesday.

A second-round leap of 7.75m was enough to see him through in eighth place.

Meanwhile, hammer thrower Angela McAuslan-Kelly progressed to the women's final, with a throw of 60.59m in the first round securing her place.

title: Jacks hits fifty as MI London seal last-ball win
description: Will Jacks hits his first half-century of this year's edition of The Hundred as MI London claim a nerve-shredding last-ball victory over Southern Brave.
fullText:
The Hundred men's competition, Utilita Bowl

Southern Brave 129-9 (100 balls): Smith 49 (26); Boult 2-15

MI London 130-7 (100 balls): Jacks 54 (41); Stoinis 3-17

Will Jacks hit his first half-century of this year's edition of The Hundred to help MI London claim a nerve-shredding last-ball win over Southern Brave.

Jacks hit three fours and two sixes in his 41-ball knock of 54 to provide the backbone of MI's chase of 130 on a tricky pitch in Southampton.

At 93-3 and with England all-rounder Jacks in good touch, MI had looked on course for a comfortable win only to lose four wickets for 34 runs.

The momentum shifted to Brave when Jacks was trapped lbw to a toe-crushing yorker from Marcus Stoinis, who had earlier removed MI skipper James Vince and Nicholas Pooran for ducks in consecutive deliveries.

Sherfane Rutherford's 21 off 12 balls swung it back the visitors' way only for a nail-biting finale as he and Rashid Khan were run out while Tom Curran was bowled by Nikhil Chaudhary.

With two runs needed from the final delivery of the match - bowled by Chaudhary - Ollie Pope managed to slash through point and scamper back for a second.

Brave had earlier posted 129-9 thanks to a 26-ball 49 from England wicketkeeper Jamie Smith at the top of the order.

Smith cracked six fours and two sixes before he chipped a slower ball from veteran seamer Richard Gleeson into the hands of long on.

Tristan Stubbs added 38 off 31 balls while Chaudhary made 13, but they were the only other Brave players to make double figures.

The wickets were shared around MI's attack with Kiwi left-arm seamer Trent Boult the pick with 2-15 as Tom Curran, Sam Curran and Gleeson also claimed two apiece.

MI are third in the standings on eight points - level with leaders Manchester Super Giants and second-placed Welsh Fire having played a game more - while Brave are second bottom having lost their first three games.

The focus switches to Headingley in The Hundred on Tuesday, where Sunrisers Leeds host Manchester Super Giants in a double header.

In the women's competition, the unbeaten Super Giants will hope to cut Southern Brave's lead at the top of the table when they face the Sunrisers at 15:00 BST.

The Super Giants' men are bidding to make it three wins from their opening three fixtures against their rivals from across the Pennines at 18:30 BST.

You can follow ball-by-ball commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app.

title: 'Nothing makes sense' - Ramsay-Peaty beaten again
description: Adam Ramsay-Peaty says "nothing makes sense" as he again has to settle for bronze at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
fullText:
Adam Ramsay-Peaty said "nothing makes sense" after he again had to settle for bronze at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

After finishing third in the 100m on Saturday, three-time Olympic champion Ramsay-Peaty, 31, was unable to keep up with the pace of Australian Sam Williamson who took his second gold with victory in the 50m.

Englishman Ramsay-Peaty, who was tearful after defeat on Saturday, was less emotional in the aftermath this time but was again unsure why he was unable to find his best times.

"I am working way too hard," he told BBC Sport.

"If those results were how much I am working then they would be a lot better.

"I need to look at that and adjust course because we are sailing in some rough seas right now and it is not sustainable.

"I have come back from worse and we will see where we end up."

'Medal dream didn't come true but my other dream is fighting brain cancer'

Whitehouse wins gymnastics gold after room-mate's horror fall

Identical twins win gymnastics medals on same day

Ramsay-Peaty is the greatest breaststroker of all time, having gone eight years unbeaten in the 100m and holding the world record in that event and the 50m.

He was the defending Commonwealth champion in the 50m and decided to continue in the sport because it was added to the 2028 Olympic schedule.

On Saturday he suggested the shorter distance would provide his best chance of a medal in Los Angeles, given his age.

"I thought I could have done better there," Ramsay-Peaty said after finishing in 26.94 seconds - 0.44secs behind Williamson.

"It is quite disappointing in terms of the time, and, as we know, times equal medals.

"I felt I could have been a little quicker, but I need to look at it and see what is going on because nothing makes sense this week to be honest."

Ramsay-Peaty dominated the events under the coaching of Mel Marshall, who relocated to Australia in 2024.

After the Paris 2024 Olympics, Ramsay-Peaty began training at Repton in Derbyshire but has since moved back to London to the tutelage of Lisa Bates.

"I am very, very happy, couldn't be happier with where I am training now," said Ramsay-Peaty.

"It is hard work, but we need to make sure that hard work is going in the right place.

"These things don't happen in three months; they happen in two years and we need to make sure we keep investing."

Meanwhile, there was gold for England's Brock Whiston in the women's 200m breaststroke SB8 final, with 15-year-old team-mate Iona Winnifrith taking bronze.

Amalie Smith, 16, took silver in the women's 200m individual medley final, and the England quartet of Freya Colbert, Abbie Wood, Leah Schlosshan and Freya Anderson won silver in the women's 4x200m freestyle relay.

title: Injured Draper withdraws on eve of another tournament
description: Former British number one Jack Draper withdraws from another event because of issues around his recurring long-term arm injury.
fullText:
Former British number one Jack Draper has withdrawn on the eve of another tournament because of the long-term arm injury which continues to cause him discomfort.

Left-handed Draper, 24, has pulled out of the ATP Tour event in Washington, which was set to be his first appearance since ruling himself out of Wimbledon last month.

Draper has been hampered by bone bruising in his serving arm for more than a year, but said at the weekend, external he was "feeling physically good" before the Mubadala DC Open.

He looked strong in practice sessions under the guidance of new coach Andy Murray, but withdrew from the ATP 500 event on Monday after feeling more soreness in the problematic arm.

It is another frustrating setback for Draper and a similar scenario to the All England Club, where he talked positively about his fitness before withdrawing just 24 hours before his first-round match.

Draper remains hopeful of playing in Montreal and Cincinnati before the US Open - where he reached the semi-finals in 2024 - starts on 30 August.

However, there is no doubt this is another concerning development - and a worrying pattern with an injury which Draper describes as "complicated".

Sabalenka & Djokovic to team up in US Open mixed doubles

Britain's Jones defends Challenger title in Palermo

The former world number four has only played 14 matches in the past 12 months, largely because of the bruised humerus which he has tried to overcome by resting for long periods.

"It's hard to tell when you can push [and] when not to push," Draper said at Wimbledon.

"At the end of the day I'm playing a very aggressive sport, that you need to play through some stuff. Sometimes it's too much. Sometimes it's not.

"I wouldn't be competing anywhere if there was a chance that I'm going to get a lot worse, for instance."

Draper's initial comeback earlier this season was derailed by tendinitis in his knee and the three-time ATP Tour winner had not played for more than two months before his return at Eastbourne in June.

Reaching the semi-finals came at a price, though, with his arm injury flaring up again at Wimbledon and leaving Draper "devastated" at having to pull out of his home Grand Slam.

Draper, who is now ranked 147th in the world, has not played a major since the US Open in August.

If he is fit enough to play at Flushing Meadows this year, he will have to come through qualifying - or be given a wildcard - to play in the main draw.

In Washington, Draper will be replaced in the draw by lucky loser Mackenzie McDonald.

title: Greaves takes 5-0 in incredible Test bowling spell
description: West Indies all-rounder Justin Greaves takes five wickets without conceding a run during an incredible spell of bowling on day three of the first Test against Pakistan.
fullText:
First Test, Tarouba (day three of five)

West Indies 311 (Hope 92; Ali 4-50) & 126-7 (Chanderpaul 35, Abbas 3-14)

Pakistan 282 (Masood 109; Greaves 5-27)

West Indies all-rounder Justin Greaves took five wickets without conceding a run in an incredible spell of bowling on day three of the first Test against Pakistan.

Greaves, who is playing in his 17th Test, claimed his maiden Test five-wicket haul to help dismiss Pakistan for 282 in response to West Indies' first-innings total of 311.

The 32-year-old Barbadian's spell - five consecutive wicket maidens - was all the more remarkable given he had bowled six overs earlier in the day for 27 runs without taking a wicket.

"When I came on captain Roston Chase just said 'continue to be disciplined in what you are doing' and to see if I can get some wickets for the team," Greaves said.

"The ball nipped around and I got some reward. Anytime I get the ball in hand the team looks to me to be that solid player for them [and] try to dig us out of situations.

"To get five wickets for the first time in Test cricket, I'm really happy, but there's still a lot of work to do in the game."

Pakistan captain Shan Masood was Greaves' first wicket at the Brian Lara Cricket Academy in Trinidad when he was bowled for 109 in the 64th over following a superb set-up.

Greaves had pushed the ball wide to the left-hander from over the wicket before he tailed a delivery back into Masood who played down the wrong line and inside edged on to his stumps.

Aamer Jamal had his middle stump uprooted in Greaves' next over as the seamer speared one through his defences.

Greaves then trapped Ali Usman lbw before he had Mohammed Rizwan and Mohammad Abbas both caught behind as Pakistan lost their last seven wickets for just 38 runs.

West Indies reached stumps on day three on 126-7 in their second innings - a lead of 155 runs - to leave the match finely poised.

title: 'Medal dream didn't come true but my other dream is fighting brain cancer'
description: Little over two years ago, Archie Goodburn's world fell apart when he was diagnosed with brain cancer - he has just competed in a Commonwealth Games final.
fullText:
Little over two years ago, Archie Goodburn's world fell apart.

The Scottish 50m breaststroke record holder was dreaming of the Paris Olympics when he checked his phone at the end of another gruelling pool session.

His training had been hindered a little in recent weeks by some odd issues. Seizures. Numbness on his left side. A feeling of deja-vu.

Test had been done and his scan results were due. So when he dried off and saw a missed call on his phone, he called back. The news that followed was devastating.

Goodburn was told he had brain cancer. He was 22 years old.

Further investigation, including biopsy surgery, revealed three 'low grade' tumours. Inoperable and unable to be removed given how they had spread through his brain.

The reality, he was told, was that he might not see his 40s.

So when Goodburn - now 25 - walked out to perhaps the loudest ovation of the week at Tollcross on Monday to compete in a Commonwealth Games final, a malestrom of emotions must have been coursing though him.

After qualifying on Sunday, tears fell. The magnitude of what had happened, of what he is doing, hit home. But by the time he stepped on the blocks for the final, the competitor had returned.

"Last night, I was so overcome to have achieved that primary goal of making the final. Then over the next 24 hours, you look for more," he told BBC Sport Scotland.

The brain cancer patient targeting Commonwealth medal this summer

The Commonwealth Games swimmer who might not see 40

MacInnes overcomes nerves to win swimming silver

The attitude is understandable. Goodburn is - astonishingly - in the best shape of his life in swimming terms. He lowered the national record to 27.12 seconds in February and qualified fifth fastest for this.

New treatments - which he fought hard to be given access to - have slowed the growth of his tumours, and he recently graduated from Edinburgh University with a first in chemical engineering.

Ultimately, he finished joint seventh - "joint last" as he put it - and missed out on the 50m breaststroke medal he craved.

But this race and this week has been about so much more than podiums and plaudits for this remarkable young man from Edinburgh, who continues to fight not only his own brain cancer, but the impact of the disease on others.

"It's pretty indescribable," he told BBC Sport Scotland when asked what the past 24 hours have been like. "Usually the words flow easily, but I'm finding myself quite speechless.

"I was really trying to soak it up, because I didn't feel like I really got much of a chance to do that after the semi. And the experience was everything I dreamed of and more. But the time, unfortunately, wasn't there."

These Games - and this summer - have been such a focus for Goodburn amid the darkness of the past two years, and he spoke afterwards about being eager to watch back the race and pore over his data as many athletes would.

He also talked about the support of his family and girlfriend Ciara Schlosshan, who competed for Scotland in the 100m butterfly just five minutes before he did.

But not many swimmers - standing wrapped in a towel, with goggles strapped to their head - would talk so passionately and eruditely about ensuring brain cancer research is properly resourced.

Team-mate Duncan Scott called Goodburn "inspirational" - and no wonder.

"I was thinking today - the goal was to make the final, and the dream was to win a medal," Goodburn said.

"That dream didn't come true, but one of my other dreams is that we see a future where brain cancer isn't the biggest killer of patients under 40.

"I advocate to try and extend my own life, but also for the other young patients and adults going through what I'm going through.

"With everything that's going on with my health, it's been difficult to think 'why am I here? Am I here to advocate as a patient advocate, or am I here to just be a professional athlete?' And it's kind of turned into a bit of both.

"I wonder how I'm going to feel off the back of this. But I know that I'm going to have memories to last a lifetime."

title: Inter in advanced talks with England defender Stones
description: England defender John Stones is in advanced talks with Inter Milan about joining the Italian side on a free transfer.
fullText:
England defender John Stones is in advanced talks with Inter Milan about joining the Italian side on a free transfer.

The centre-half is a free agent after leaving Manchester City at the end of June.

Stones has been the subject of major interest from clubs across Europe, including Chelsea and Juventus.

But Serie A champions Inter have held positive discussions with the 32-year-old and are understood to be leading the race to sign the Premier League and Champions League winner on a two-year contract.

Stones made 295 appearances for City after joining from Everton for £47.5m in 2016.

He helped City win six Premier League titles, the Champions League, two FA Cups, five League Cups, three Community Shields, the Club World Cup and the Uefa Super Cup.

The former Barnsley defender has won 93 international caps and was part of the England squad who finished third at the World Cup.
